World.title: Former FIFA Vice President Prince Ali accuses Infantino of 'blackmail' as presure on leadership mounts
World.content:
Former FIFA vice president Prince Ali bin Al Hussein was the latest football figure to criticise the leadership of Gianni Infantino on Tuesday, whose re-election is becoming increasingly uncertain.

 

Prince Ali, the third son of King Hussein of Jordan, said the Jordanian federation he leads still has not been paid money due for reaching the final of the FIFA Arab Cup played last December in Qatar.

In a social media post, Prince Ali said that during the World Cup — where Jordan made its debut in June — he was told if he endorsed FIFA President Gianni Infantino “it would go a long way to helping our FA out.”

Infantino is under pressure to save his 11-year presidency amid a fierce backlash from global soccer leaders about his now-failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

“We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now,” said Prince Ali, who placed third in a five-candidate FIFA presidential contest when Infantino was first elected in February 2016.

“But the whole situation amounts to blackmail and we refuse to give in to that,” the Jordanian royal wrote Tuesday.

The 2025 FIFA Arab Cup that Jordan lost in the title match against Morocco was set to pay $4.2 million to the beaten finalist, Jordanian media reported last year.

“The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet,” Prince Ali wrote, “while at the same time FIFA brags about how many billions they have in reserve.”

“It is clear the problem really is with leadership. For months, FIFA has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters,” he said.

Fallout from his secretive private equity plan revealed one week ago has rocked soccer politics with Infantino’s former colleagues at European soccer body UEFA now looking for a rival candidate.

FIFA has set an 18 November deadline for candidates to declare for the election by 211 member federations on 18 March in Rabat, Morocco.

World.title: WHO calls for more support to tackle Ebola outbreak
World.content:
The World Health Organization (WHO) on Tuesday called for greater support to tackle the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), warning that the response is still struggling to keep pace with the spread of the disease.

 

"The outbreak is unfortunately still expanding beyond the capacity of the response," WHO spokesman Tarik Jasarevic told reporters in Geneva.

"We need more support in terms of finances, but also other resources to scale up all areas of response: treatment capacity, field investigation teams, safe burial teams and community workers."

The Country has recorded 3,802 confirmed Ebola cases, including 1,707 deaths. A further 727 patients have recovered, while 275 suspected cases remain under investigation.

Around 17,000 contacts are being monitored, with more than 80% receiving daily follow-up checks.

Although cases have been reported in five provinces, nearly 90% are in the northeastern province of Ituri, with almost all the remainder in neighbouring North Kivu.

Related First Bundibugyo Ebola vaccine to start human trials in the UK

Jasarevic said the response must focus on where the virus is spreading now and where it could spread next.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that spreads through close contact with infected people and their bodily fluids.

The DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak on 15 May after several deaths were reported in Ituri.

The outbreak is being driven by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no proven safe and effective treatments, vaccines or post-exposure prophylaxis options.

However, several trials of potential therapies, vaccines and post-exposure antiviral drugs are under way.

Vasee Moorthy, who heads the WHO's research and development blueprint programme, said the early results were promising.

World.title: More than 170 migrants rescued after boat catches fire in English Channel
World.content:
A major rescue operation took place on Tuesday to assist more than 170 people attempting to cross from France to the United Kingdom, authorities in both countries said. It was one of the largest operations of its kind since records began in 2018.

 

The inflatable boat was still in the French search and rescue zone when its engine caught fire, causing the vessel to begin breaking apart, the maritime prefecture for the English Channel and the North Sea said. The incident "forced its occupants to jump into the water", the Pas-de-Calais prefecture added.

French authorities then deployed two rescue vessels, a navy helicopter and medical teams. The Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), a charity specialising in sea rescue, and the UK Border Force also took part in the operation.

No one was killed in the incident. French teams rescued 103 people, while the remaining 54 were rescued by British crews. All were brought ashore at the port of Boulogne-sur-Mer to receive medical care and assistance.

The boat had left the Normandy village of Veules-les-Roses at around 6 am, French authorities and the RNLI said. From the moment it set off, it was monitored by French rescue services.

Risking lives to cross

French maritime authorities said migrants attempting the crossing in makeshift, overloaded boats often refuse rescue unless faced with an immediate danger.

Rescuers do not force people off the boats because of the risk of capsizing that would put people's lives at risk, the statement said.

The boats are often overloaded. French maritime authorities said the average number of people crammed into these vessels has risen from 26 in 2021 to 65 since the start of this year.

In recent weeks, witnesses in France have reported seeing larger-than-usual boats crossing the Channel, measuring around 12 metres in length, compared with the usual eight to ten metres.

Last week, four people died in two separate attempts to cross the Channel on small boats.

Since the start of the year, at least 14 people have lost their lives attempting the crossing, according to an AFP tally based on official French and UK sources.

At least 29 migrants lost their lives last year, according to a similar AFP count.

A sharp drop in attempted crossings

The UK government is showing "unwavering determination" to tackle the issue, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said. "Progress is being made, but we are not letting our guard down," he added.

In a bid to stem the crossings, London and Paris signed a multi-million-euro agreement earlier this year. It includes reinforced police patrols and surveillance along France's northern coastline.

The package also deploys new technologies to tackle "taxi boats": small, usually inflatable motorised craft used by smugglers to pick up migrants along the northern French coast.

"The number of crossings has fallen by 50% this year compared with the same period in 2025," Andy Burnham said.

"The July we have just experienced is even the month with the lowest number of crossings in six years. Clearly there is progress, but we are not resting on our laurels. We will continue our efforts relentlessly."

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said an estimated 10,000 migrants have crossed the Channel from France to Britain since the beginning of the year, compared with 24,000 in the same period last year. The number of successful crossing attempts is 160 this year, down from 413, he said.

An increasingly prominent issue in Europe

Irregular migrant arrivals have been an issue faced by multiple UK governments in recent years. They have also boosted support for the far-right Reform UK party, led by Nigel Farage.

"We must address this problem rather than turn it into a matter of party politics," Andy Burnham said, adding that he wants to "take back control of the situation" and "bring in changes that will reassure the public".

He insisted that Britons do not want a border that appears to be out of control. "We must regain control of our borders while continuing to provide support to people who genuinely need protection," he added.

World.title: From TikTok videos to political claims: How misleading information spread during the Ceuta crisis
World.content:
Before around 70,000 people crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, which borders Morocco, videos promising an easier route to Europe reportedly spread on TikTok, Facebook and other social media platforms.

 

Reports say some claimed the border was open, while others suggested migrants arriving by sea could not be immediately returned.

Others posted pictures of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, framing him as a leader who would give “dignity and recognition to those who build Spain”, highlighting a recent programme by the Spanish government to regularise thousands of migrants — without explaining that it only applied to those already living in the country.

As videos emerged showing thousands gathering at the shorelines, a second wave of misleading claims emerged, this time about what had caused the crossings and what would happen to those who reached Spain.

Here is a look at some of the biggest claims and what the evidence shows so far.

Claim: Spain had relaxed its migration rules

It remains unclear what exactly triggered the unprecedented surge into Ceuta, with officials and experts pointing to a combination of factors including economic hardship in Morocco, social media misinformation, criminal networks and the actions of authorities on both sides of the border.

Sánchez has argued that migrant smugglers deliberately misrepresented a recent Supreme Court ruling to encourage people to cross, whilst migration and human rights activists say rumours of the events, which spread on social media, helped fuel the sudden surge.

In the days before the crossings, social media posts claimed that Spain had effectively relaxed its migration rules, focusing on two genuine developments: a decision taken by Spain to regularise thousands of migrants and the Supreme Court ruling.

Critics, including the US State Department, argued that Spain’s regularisation programme encouraged the mass crossings by signalling the country was now lenient on immigration.

The programme, which has been misconstrued and subject to misinformation since its announcement, only applied to undocumented migrants who were living in Spain since 1 January 2026 and met residency requirements. It would therefore not apply to those who arrived in Ceuta at the end of July and in early August.

At the same time, misleading posts also circulated about the recent Spanish Supreme Court judgment concerning migrants intercepted after arriving by sea.

This ruling did not grant migrants the right to remain in Spain but found that migrants intercepted after arriving by sea could not be immediately returned under the special border regime used at Ceuta and its sister city, Melilla, and instead had to go through Spain’s ordinary legal returns system.

This judgment only applied to the legal procedure and did not give migrants the automatic right to remain in Spain or continue to mainland Europe.

Although Sánchez’s government has encouraged a regularisation programme for undocumented migrants already living in Spain, it has maintained a tougher approach to irregular migration, particularly in Ceuta and Melilla.

Sánchez’s government has not repealed the 2015 border rejection provision for Ceuta and Melilla, has continued close cooperation with Morocco on migration control, and has provided financial and operational support to help Moroccan authorities prevent irregular crossings.

Spanish politicians have also accused Rabat of allowing people to cross, pointing to limited border enforcement. An Associated Press photographer reported they witnessed Moroccan officers standing aside before security forces later intervened.

Morocco has since argued that it warned Spain that the Supreme Court ruling could encourage more people to attempt the crossing, arguing that trafficking networks would exploit the decision online — which Spain denies.

On Tuesday, the EU's migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, also expressed concern about the role of online disinformation in the crisis, although he stopped short of identifying a specific source or actor behind it.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain line up for food distribution on a beach in the Spanish territory of Ceuta, 3 August 2026 Bernat Armangue/AP

Claim: Migrants who reached Ceuta would continue to mainland Europe

As thousands of people entered Ceuta, politicians and commentators across Europe warned that the migrants would soon continue to mainland Spain and other European countries.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni temporarily introduced checks on air and sea arrivals from Spain, while French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced plans to strengthen border controls. British politicians, including former Home Secretary Suella Braverman, also claimed the migrants would be heading towards the rest of Europe.

However, contrary to these claims, Magnus Brunner, the EU’s migration commissioner, said "not a single person" had crossed into mainland Europe on Friday evening, adding that the Schengen Borders Code already provides for additional border checks on people travelling from Ceuta and Melilla.

Spain’s foreign ministry has affirmed that checks are carried out on exit by sea or air, the only routes available. This means that no one can travel from the Spanish territories to mainland Spain without being identified by National Police.

It also said that illegal entry into Ceuta doesn’t give migrants the right to remain in Spain or the right to travel to the EU mainland.

Additionally, Spanish authorities have said the majority of migrants who entered Ceuta have already returned to Morocco, either voluntarily or after being expelled.

As of the time of publishing, several thousand migrants remain in the enclave and, according to the Associated Press, hope to hold out and reach mainland Spain.

Those who remain face an uncertain legal future, could eventually be sent back, or face a legal limbo and possibly spells in government-run centres. According to Spanish law, adult migrants who apply for asylum face expulsion procedures if rejected, while unaccompanied minors are entitled to legal protection.

Claim: The crossings were organised by Israel and the US as retaliation

As the crisis unfolded, conspiracy theories emerged online claiming the mass crossings had been orchestrated as retaliation for Spain's criticism of Israel's military campaign in Gaza and its condemnation of joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

Some posts alleged that Israel or the United States had encouraged Morocco to allow migrants to cross into Ceuta in an effort to punish the Spanish government for its foreign policy.

There is, however, so far little evidence to support these theories that either the US or Israel were involved in encouraging people to cross into Ceuta.

World.title: Spain says 70,000 of 72,000 migrants who crossed into Ceuta have already returned
World.content:
Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska has said that 72,000 migrants have entered Ceuta since last Thursday, adding that 70,000 of them have already returned to Morocco.

 

During his appearance, he also stressed that the National Intelligence Centre (CNI) had not warned of the possibility of a migration crisis of this magnitude, in which more than 80 people lost their lives while trying to cross the border. He also said that his European counterparts had backed the Spanish government's actions and acknowledged the "effectiveness" of the response deployed.

Grande-Marlaska spoke after the extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers, held by videoconference on Tuesday at the request of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and backed by 22 member states. At the end of the meeting, EU countries expressed their "strong solidarity" with Spain over the events in Ceuta and pledged to strengthen European early-warning and alert mechanisms for this type of crisis.

The minister described the meeting as "absolutely constructive" and said that the "effective and immediate" response of the Spanish authorities had been acknowledged during the session. However, several of the 22 countries that pushed for the meeting had previously voiced concerns about how risks are managed on Europe's southern border.

According to Grande-Marlaska, one of the points made clear during the meeting was that Ceuta has a special status within the Schengen area, meaning that no one can leave the autonomous city without undergoing an effective document check.

Grande-Marlaska said on Tuesday that the National Intelligence Centre (CNI) had not warned of an episode similar to the one experienced in 2021. During the press conference following the extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers, Marlaska defended the work of the CNI and the intelligence services, praising their efforts.

Related Spanish government received intelligence warnings of Ceuta migrant surge according to a report

The interior minister insisted that, had there been an alert about a scenario comparable to that of May 2021, when around 10,000 people entered Ceuta in just a few hours, the information would have reached the highest levels of the state. "That did not happen," he concluded.

An extra €25 million for Ceuta

The government will allocate an additional €25 million to Ceuta to strengthen support for unaccompanied migrant minors who have arrived in the city during the recent migration crisis. The announcement was made on Tuesday by Spain's Minister for Inclusion, Social Security and Migration and government spokesperson, Elma Saiz.

The new funding comes on top of the €5.5 million approved last July at the Sectoral Conference on Children and Adolescents. As the minister explained, the aim is to ensure an appropriate response to the situation facing the autonomous city.

"The government has been and will continue to be at Ceuta's side, especially with the most vulnerable," Saiz said during a press conference.

Elma Saiz during a Cabinet meeting in 2024 Flickr - La Moncloa

Saiz also called on all the autonomous regions, including those governed by the Popular Party, to help receive and care for unaccompanied migrant minors.

The government spokesperson also reiterated that the executive had "never" received any report anticipating the scale of the migration crisis that unfolded in Ceuta last Thursday, although it had been working on forecasts of an increase in irregular arrivals over the summer.

Saiz was responding to reports published on Monday citing sources at Morocco's Foreign Ministry, according to which Rabat had warned Spain days earlier about the possible consequences of a Supreme Court ruling handed down at the beginning of July.

The minister praised Morocco's cooperation, describing it as key to delivering an "exceptional response" to the emergency, and pointed to the meeting of EU interior ministers, in which Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska took part on Tuesday.

She also highlighted the support expressed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who on Monday praised Spain's handling of the migration crisis.

Two educational centres to support minors

For their part, sources at the Ministry of Youth and Children said that, in coordination with the Ministry of Education, two educational centres have been made available in Ceuta to accommodate unaccompanied migrant minors, with particular attention to girls.

The same sources said that the Minister for Youth and Children, Sira Rego, will travel to the autonomous city in the coming days to monitor the situation and activate all the resources needed to ensure a dignified reception for children and adolescents.

The planned measures also include implementing the reform of the Immigration Act, which provides for a system to relocate unaccompanied minors from territories under high migratory pressure, such as Ceuta, to other autonomous regions.

World.title: White House revokes visa of Brazil's ambassador to US: reports
World.content:
The move was in response to Brazil delaying formal diplomatic approval of the US ambassador to Brasilia and denying visas to several US diplomats.

The administration of Donald Trump has moved to revoke the visa of Brazil's ambassador to the US, sources in the State Department told media outlets on Tuesday.

Ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti's visa revocation was reportedly in response to the denial of visas to two American diplomats who sought to visit Brazil ahead of upcoming elections.

The US has also accused the Brazilian government of stalling Trump's ambassadorial choice to the South American country.

What do we know so far about the visa revocation?

State Department officials reportedly said the decision could be quickly reversed if Brazil takes appropriate action and accepts Trump's ambassadorial choice.

The Associated Press cited one State Department official as saying on condition of anonymity that despite the revocation of her visa, Viotti is not being expelled from the US.

"The action was that the ​visa of a senior diplomat here was revoked or canceled. That is not the same thing as kicking the person out of ​the country. It means that they are here but without a visa, and would have their ​visa restored if ‌the balance is restored by giving agrément to our chosen ambassadorial nominee," a State Department official was quoted by the Reuters news agency as saying.

Despite the move, the State Department official reportedly stressed Washington's valuing of the relationship with Brazil and its respect for the Brazilian people in whatever government they choose through free and fair elections in Brazil.

"We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues," the official said.

World.title: New Gaza peace plan: Will US pressure Israel to accede?
World.content:
Reports suggest US President Donald Trump would be "very disappointed" if Israel doesn't agree to a new peace plan for Gaza, announced last week. But how far would the US go to make that happen?

US President Donald Trump touted it as a "historic breakthrough."

But so far the new Gaza peace deal, announced last week and meant to help end the fighting and ease the ongoing humanitarian crisis in the coastal enclave, only seems to have resulted in another standoff between the key belligerents.

However, experts point out, there are some differences between this new peace deal and previous arrangements that could be positive.

For one thing, it is much more detailed and substantive. For another, statements by Trump indicate he might be more willing to push Israel towards accepting the deal. And finally, after resisting the idea for years, this month the Gaza-based group Hamas has agreed to disarm.

It was Hamas that sent fighters into Israel on October 7, 2023, an attack that resulted in over 1,000 deaths and sparked nearly three years of an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza. The Israeli military has since killed over 73,000 people there, causing a UN independent commission of inquiry to classify its behavior as a genocide.

UN report condemns Israeli military action in Gaza To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of the main sticking points of any peace plan for Gaza has been the sequencing of events. Israel has demanded that Hamas disarm before it withdraws its troops from Gaza. But up until last month, Hamas had refused to disarm until Israel withdrew its troops. This led to an ongoing stalemate.

Early in July, Hamas agreed to hand over power to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, or NCAG, a group of independent technocrats set up to govern Gaza. Later in July, the group also agreed to hand over their weapons to the NCAG.

Why did Hamas do this?

Hamas agreeing to disarm after years of promoting armed resistance against Israel should be taken seriously, says Muhammad Shehada, a visiting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa program at the European Council of Foreign Affairs, who is originally from Gaza.

Hamas has been under pressure from negotiators from other countries like Egypt and Qatar and this could also be something of a political tactic "to expose that Israel is the party that is obstructing any progress in Gaza under [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's government," Shehada concedes.

But, he added, "they would not have made such a major, historic concession unless their backs were totally against the wall and they fully understood that this is the only way forward."

Should Israel agree to the new peace plan, there would also be no way Hamas could renege.

"They would be locked in," Shehada told DW. "Because if they renege or violate the decommissioning arrangements, they would give Israel the ultimate pretext to resume military operations in Gaza and collapse the whole Trump deal. Hamas would then be blamed by the entire Palestinian public."

On the other hand, Hamas probably also understands that Israel is unlikely to agree, so there's no fear disarmament is going to happen immediately, he added.

The dangers of living along Gaza's shifting front lines To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Israel's political problem with peace plan

Israel expressed its displeasure with the new 15-point deal almost immediately.

"The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel's positions," a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister's office told news agency AFP.

Far-right Israeli minister Itamar Ben-Gvir dismissed the deal as "unacceptable" on social media, adding that "assassinations in Gaza must continue."

Israel will hold elections in October and Netanyahu faces tough competition. If he makes any concessions on Gaza, he would likely face a public outcry and a lack of potential coalition partners from the far right.

"Netanyahu faces a critical election in less than 90 days from now and although there may be some flexibility on other issues like Lebanon or Iran, he cannot appear flexible on Hamas," explains Aaron David Miller, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. "The shadow of October 7 hangs heavy and dark on Israel, and will for a very long time."

Until elections happen, Netanyahu will try to sabotage any kind of Gaza peace deal because it would be "political suicide" for him, Shehada adds.

After a Monday meeting between Netanyahu and the US-led Board of Peace, it was announced that Hamas' disarming and an Israeli withdrawal would now not happen in phases, as the new 15-point plan had detailed. Gradual progress would have given each side time to build trust, observers argued.

But after the Israeli complaints, the plan seemed to revert back to absolutes: Israel would only be asked to withdraw once Hamas was completely disarmed.

Would US pressure Israel?

There is really only one way to change this and that would be via pressure from the US, Shehada and other experts say.

"Israel … will be under enormous pressure from Trump to go along or risk his ire by sabotaging what he is touting as a historic success," Alan Pino, a senior fellow with the Atlantic Council's Middle East programs wrote in an op-ed for the US think tank last week.

There has been some evidence of pressure from Trump. For example, when the US President released the 15-point plan, reports suggest he did so without showing it to Israel first.

Following the plan's release, a senior US official gave reporters an off-the-record briefing and suggested Trump would be "very, very disappointed" if Israel did not go along with the new plan.

And, as Miller points out, "Donald Trump has said things and done things to Israel, and to an Israeli prime minister, that none of his predecessors have ever done. Nobody talked to an Israeli prime minister the way that Trump has talked to Netanyahu. Nobody opened a dialogue with Hamas without checking with the Israelis."

Expert Aaron David Miller says that no US president ever 'leaked the private contents of their phone conversations with the Israeli prime minister (pictured left), profanity laced, mocking him' – but Trump (right) did Image: Maayan Toaf/GPO/Handout/Anadolu/IMAGO

All of that is unprecedented, Miller told DW. "But whether Donald Trump would be willing to impose significant and serious costs on the US-Israeli relationship is another matter altogether," he told DW.

That could include things like cutting or restricting US assistance or intelligence cooperation and not defending Israel at the UN and other forums. But, Miller and Shehada both point out, none of that has happened.

"When you get between Donald Trump and something he really cares about, that's a very bad and dangerous place to be," Miller continued. "So you have to ask, what is it that that Donald Trump cares so much about that he'd be prepared to really pressure Israel? Maybe an Israel-Saudi relationship down the road, if we were on the cusp of a real breakthrough in Gaza."

But the current reality is so far removed from that, that it's unlikely Trump will move beyond words, Miller concluded. He's also more likely to be more focused on using any leverage to extricate himself from the Iran war, the former adviser to the US State Department noted.

World.title: Italy: Garbage workers help woman find €1 million jackpot
World.content:
A woman who won €1 million mistakenly threw her lottery ticket in a trash bin in Bitonto, southern Italy — prompting her local sanitation company to launch an hourslong search.

Garbage workers in the city of Bitonto, Italy recovered a €1 million ($1.15 million) lottery ticket, after having to search through an entire truck full of trash. Waste management company SANB administrator Roberto Nicola Toscano told AFP news agency that the ticket was found "miraculously still in one piece."

Toscano received the panicked call from the woman who had won the big prize and lost it.

The unnamed woman entered the Saturday lottery and on Sunday she went to check her ticket's result at her local shop.

But the machine read "non-payable," a common message indicating the prize was too large for the small retailer to redeem. She mistook the message to say that there were no winnings.

"The winner always played the same numbers, as they were associated with a loved one," Toscano said. According to Italian newspaper Corriere Della Sera, the woman's winning combination was 2, 4, 8, 10, and 51. A family member of the woman noticed the combination was the winning one and informed her, but she had already discarded the ticket.

By the time they returned to the shop, a garbage truck had already collected the trash bin that held her ticket.

How did was the ticket found?

After SANB was contacted by the woman, the garbage company moved quickly to reconstruct the journey of the ticket, Toscano told AFP. They were able to identify the correct truck and stopped it.

Combing through collected trash would pose the risk of potentially dangerous material in the waste, so the vehicle was taken to a special site equipped to do the search, Toscano said.

It took the workers one day of "working in conditions that were anything but pleasant" to find the ticket, Toscano told Corriere Della Sera.

Toscano said the woman cried when she found out, over the phone, that the ticket was found.

He told the paper that professionalism, organization, and a great deal of luck made the moment happen, saying the impossible result could not have happened without the garbage workers.

As a SANB is a public entity, the cost of the search would be covered by taxpayers, but Toscano told AFP that the woman had promised to "cover all of the additional costs."

World.title: Who is responsible for the Ceuta border surge?
World.content:
Tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta several days ago. DW interviewed two experts to understand what may have caused the incident.

For a long time, the Moroccan government chose not to comment on the Ceuta border crisisthat saw tens of thousands of migrants surging into the Spanish exclave on the African continent. It was not until Sunday that Moroccan interior ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi said "the malicious exploitation of the digital space," "misleading information" and misinterpretations of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling were to blame for the incident. Morocco has since said it never intended for the border surge to happen and has promised full cooperation with Spain.

Spain, however, was quick to suspect Moroccan involvement, with Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calling the border breach an "attack on our territorial sovereignty." Videos have, after all, surfaced showing Moroccan security forces doing nothing to stop the crowd surging forward.

Efforts have been made to try and explain what caused the migrant crisis. Some have said Spain's recent rapprochement with Algeria may have angered Marocco, while others have speculated US influence may have played a role, although there is no reliable evidence to support the latter theory.

A complex situation

DW spoke with two analysts who caution against simplistic explanations. They do, however, ascribe different degrees of responsibility to Marocco for causing the crisis.

"I think the situation today is significantly different from what it was in 2021," says Isabelle Werenfels, a Maghreb regional expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). Back then, Morocco was interested in exerting foreign policy pressure on Spain over the Western Sahara dispute, she says. Today, Moroccowould have "a great deal to lose, above all, international credibility and investment" if found to have deliberately orchestrated the Ceuta migrant surge.

Jochen Oltmer, a migration researcher at the University of Osnabrück in Germany, also warns against jumping to conclusions, telling DW "you have to keep in mind the many different interests at play." He points to Ceuta's unique status as a European exclave on the African continent, decades of migration flows, the impact of social networks, and the hopes of many migrants to build better lives abroad.

A variety of factors account for the Ceuta migrant surge Image: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Oltmer says Moroccan authorities carry considerable responsibility for the Ceuta crisis, as "such a border crossing could never have taken place if the Moroccan side hadn't looked the other way." It was this inaction that made possible a border breach of this magnitude in the first place, he told DW.

Werenfels does not dispute this assessment. Yet she also believes Morocco may have wanted to send a political signal to Spain, perhaps over its recent rapprochement with Algeria and its decision to grant Spanish citizenship to individuals born in Western Sahara before September 1977.

Western Sahara: Caught between sovereignty and struggle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"But there is a significant difference between making a political statement and orchestrating a migration surge on this scale," Werenfels says. The expert thinks it is "unlikely" that Morocco had planned the latter, even though it cannot be ruled out, while stressing a lot of information remains extremely unclear-

Who bears responsibility?

There is some evidence to suggest that Morocco played a part in the border surge to push its own political agenda, says Oltmer. For years, the country has viewed itself as an indispensable partner to the European Union in the context of migration policy, he says, adding that Morocco has repeatedly emphasized how much the bloc depends on its cooperation. Yet the conflict over Western Sahara, and Morocco's rivalry with Algeria, also plays an important role, Oltmer explains. That is why he "ultimately cannot imagine that the recent events would have been possible without Morocco."

Werenfels advocates for a more nuanced analysis. She suspects it's possible that Morocco wanted to send a message but that matters got out of control. Werenfels says it is hard to imagine that Morocco would want to risk a lasting rift with Spain and the European Union. This is all the more true given that Morocco will be hosting the next football World Cup together with Spain and Portugal, and also depends on Spanish gas supplies. In 2025, one-quarter of Spain's total natural gas exports went to Morocco.

Even if Morocco had wanted to send a political message, that does not automatically mean that it deliberately orchestrated a migration surge of this magnitude, Werenfels says. Doing so would carry enormous political and economic risk.

No evidence of third-party involvement

Neither of the experts believe a third country played a part in the Ceuta migration crisis. That said, Werenfels does entertain the possibility that other governments or political actors may have attempted to exploit the situation propagandistically for their own political interests and thereby may have amplified the crisis.

Werenfels also says it remains unclear how the situation escalated so quickly. There is much to suggest that news of an alleged border opening spread very quickly, prompting numerous young Moroccans to spontaneously set off for Ceuta. It is also possible that, given these circumstances, some Moroccan security personnel did not intervene.

Both scholars agree on the root causes of migration. "It's about hope and expectations for the future," says Oltmer. Moroccans have been emigrating for many decades, with family and friendship networks in Europe making it easier for people to risk moving abroad, he says.

Spanish soldiers escort migrants back to the border Image: Antonio Sempere/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Werenfels also points out social and economic factors driving emigration. She says that while Morocco had made progress in recent years, many young people are hardly seeing improvements in their everyday lives. The scholar says Marocco's education and health care sectors show particularly significant shortcomings. This lack of prospects compels many to risk migrating abroad, Werenfels says.

Overall, both experts agree that the Ceuta migrant crisis was not brought about by a single political decision, or conspiracy theory, for that matter. The incident instead resulted from the interplay of geopolitical tensions, migration policy agendas, and the often precarious circumstances of many young Moroccans.

This article was translated from German

World.title: Middle East: India says commercial ship sunk off Yemen
World.content:
08/04/2026 August 4, 2026 India: Continuing attacks on shipping 'deeply worrisome'

India's Foreign Ministry called for restoring free and safe navigation.

"The continuing incidents of attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply worrisome," the ministry said.

"The targeting of commercial shipping in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways in the region, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest," it said.

India is a major importer of oil, petroleum, natural gas and other goods from the Gulf region, and is directly connected to the region via the Arabian Sea. It is therefore one of the countries hardest hit by the economic disruption from the US-Iran war.

India currently contributes more than 300,000 seafarers to the global shipping industry , which is more than 10% of the global total, second only to the Philippines.

World.title: South Sudan: How climate change can result in toxic water
World.content:
Years of flooding have resulted in disastrous water pollution in South Sudan's main oil region. As communities, scientists and health workers scramble for solutions, the long-term impacts of the crisis is yet to emerge.

The village of Bentiu has seen it all: Located in the north of South Sudan near the border with Sudan, the capital of Unity State used to have a population of merely several thousand people.

But war, violence and other crisis have resulted in an additional 140,000 displaced persons seeking shelter there since 2013, resulting in the establishment of a massive camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs).

Several UN bodies including the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) are active on the ground, running what is known as the Protection of Civilians (POC) camp, which by now feels more like a permanent structure.

In South Sudan, usable water is increasingly becoming a rare commodity Image: UIG/IMAGO

At a makeshift pier, children are seen playing, countless canoes bring in fish to feed scores of people at the camp, where food insecurity remains a chief concern.

Immediately, each day's yield is separated into two categories: One stock with fresh, healthy fish, and another for those believed to be contaminated.

Simon Gatkuoth, a camp resident in his early forties, lifts a fish from a wheelbarrow, explaining that fish that are caught near the oil fields are contaminated: "When we cook them, the soup sometimes smells like penicillin," he says.

"But there is no option. We have to eat. We cannot stop eating because there is no alternative."

Fish in the polluted waters are often discarded if they show signs of contamination Image: Marco Simoncelli

Flood waters that just won't recede

Viewed from the sky, the POC Camp resembles an artificial island in the midst of a region that has been transformed into what appears to be a gigantic lake.

Here, the largely nomadic communities of South Sudan's Unity State have long adapted their lives to the seasonal floods that shape life in what is one of the world's largest wetlands known as the Sudd.

But in 2021, and unprecedented deluge of floods linked to climate change submerged farmland across the region, destroying livelihoods and killing thousands of cattle.

Just one year earlier, authorities in neighboring Uganda had issued a warning that rising levels in Lake Victoria, situated roughly 1,000 kilometers (650 miles) to the south, would require the release of large volumes of water into the White Nile river, which flows past Bentiu.

But South Sudan, one of the poorest countries, lacked the dams, flood-control systems and water-management infrastructure needed to cope with the flooding, leaving many communities highly vulnerable to flooding.

To this day, the waters from that flood are yet to recede.

Satellite images show the ongoing devastation of the 2021 floods, with oil wells remaining under water for years Image: Placemarks. Map Data: Google/Airbus

Oil and water do not mix

Maintained by the IOM, a simple levee is all that separates the POC Camp from the flooded plain; without constant maintenance, it would give way to the water.

The people here appear weary: First displaced by war and later hit by floods, most now depend on humanitarian aid, trapped somewhere between continuously rising water levels and unresolved conflict.

Yet in recent years, another disaster has slowly emerged, linking the devastating 2021 flooding to a major environmental hazard: Unity State, where the Bentiu POC Camp is located, is the South Sudan's biggest oil producing region.

Oil makes up more than 90% of state revenue, and accounts for nearly all of the country's exports. It is a vital sector for the country's battling economy, which has been severely limited in recent years by the war in Sudan to its north, with pipelines limited to a trickle, and many reserves sitting untapped or unused.

A geospatial analysis found that during the devastating 2021 floods, 159 out of over 400 oil wells in the region were submerged under water, amounting to around 41% of oil extraction infrastructure in the area.

Water levels around Bentiu do not seem to want to subside, even years after the devastating floods Image: Marco Simoncelli

In a joint effort with PlaceMarks Africa — an organization which makes of satellite imagery to help "design solutions for contemporary challenges" on the continent, DW has found that more than 50 of these wells continue to be submerged to this day — a growing cause for concern.

The rivers and lakes that hundreds of thousands depend on for drinking water, cooking and fishing appear to have been contaminated by the oil fields, with could carry potentially long-term consequences for both local ecosystems and human health.

"Many animals are dying because of this pollution, and people are also suffering from symptoms they attribute to it. All of this is visible, but we do not yet have sufficient evidence or epidemiological studies to state it with certainty," explains researcher Marko Gatkuoth, who is attached to the Rift Valley Institute — an independent research organization operating primarily in Central and Eastern Africa.

"The flood that began more than four years ago has become a vector of pollution. It has made the contaminants mobile."

'Deliberate negligence'

Bul Duot Kuer, a South Sudanese researcher at Kenyatta University in Kenya, has conducted extensive research on the environmental impact of oil production in Unity State.

In a recent study, he identified lead concentrations of up to 18 micrograms per liter in the rivers around Bentiu and nearby Rotriak — nearly double the guideline value set by the World Health Organization (WHO). He also found hydrocarbon concentrations in the water at more than five times above the recommended limits.

Bul Duot Kuer blames the government for remaining inactive duing the growing water crisis Image: Marco Simoncelli

"Water is the most polluted element," says Kuer. "There is no control. The environmental laws are there on paper, but they are simply not being enforced. This is negligence. The government and the oil companies do not care about people's health."

Waters around the settlement of Rotriak are particularly affect by this oil contamination: Satellite imagery analysed by PlaceMarks exposed pipelines, wells and abandoned facilities scattered across the settlement.

This is an area were children play among rusty pipes and women wash laundry at a former retention pond for oil production wastewater — albeit typically not by choice: Local resident Anna Nyashing Bul told DW that she and her family had to evacuate to Rotriak "because it was the only place that remained dry" after the 2021 flooding.

The untreated water they rely on often has "black film on the surface," she explains, which has repeatedly made her family fall sick.



"But we had nothing else to drink."

Despite widespread pollution, the region around Roriak has seen massive urban sprawling in recent years due to ongoing population displacement Image: Placemarks. Map Data: Google/Airbus

Birth defects and miscarriages

Meanwhile at Bentiu State Hospital, staff have noticed an increase of children born with deformities and other birth defects.

Midwives interviewed by DW also describe an apparent increase in miscarriages, complicated deliveries and congenital anomalies in recent years — especially with mothers who come from areas located in and around the oil fields.

19-year-old Nyapuka Nios from Rotriak just gave birth days ago; her newborn presents visible malformations to the hands and upper lip.

"I don't know what will happen to him," she whispers. "It is God's will. God gave him to me this way."

In another room, Nyekal Nuok watches over her baby girl, who was born with spina bifida five days earlier. She also lived in Rotriak during most of her pregnancy.

South Sudan: Lack of access to safe drinking water To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Research has shown that women living near oil wells are more likely to give birth to children with congenital anomalies.

Dorgan Patai, Director of Health Services in Rubkona County agrees that "since the floods, we are seeing more miscarriages and more children born with malformations," adding that "in the long term, this could even lead to infertility."

However, there has been no comprehensive investigation to establish whether these cases are indeed linked to environmental contamination.

The WHO says that a review of routine health surveillance data failed to present any statistically relevant increase in miscarriages, complications or other anomalies in Unity State, stressing that anecdotal reports should be interpreted cautiously.

Health workers in the region worry about a rise in birth defects, which is believed to be linked to oil pollution in the water Image: Antonio Lacerda/dpa/picture alliance

Dead in the water

There are few people who have done more to hold South Sudanese authorities accountable for the environmental consequences of oil production than Ayen Mijok Kiir, First Deputy Speaker of the Council of States, which is South Sudan's upper house of parliament.

Ayen Mijok Kiir keeps fighting for justice for the thousands of people who have no access to clean water Image: Marco Simoncelli

She believes that years of conflict and insecurity have pushed issues like environmental protection and public health down the list of national priorities.

"We are not a stable country," Kiir highlights. "There are challenges in allocating resources to different sectors. We are under pressure to prioritise security. But yes, even with these challenges, we should have done more."

With her tireless campaigning, she succeeded in encouraging President Salva Kiir to further investigate the potential link between deformities at birth and oil-related pollution in 2024 despite many other ongoing crises in the region.

But despite numerous ministerial meetings being held, nothing seems to change.

"What difference will it make if I talk about this yet again?" she s ays quietly. "I have spoken about it so much, given so many interviews, and nothing has happened."

Ultimately, South Sudan still lacks effective environmental monitoring and public health standard in its oil producing areas — 15 years after gaining independence.

With conflict and suffering remaining rife throughout the region, addressing the affects of global warming might remain an elusive goal, as South Sudan struggles on many fronts to keep its head above water.

World.title: What does Zambia's opposition stand without Edgar Lungu?
World.content:
The death of former President Edgar Lungu reshaped opposition politics in Zambia ahead of the August 13 general election. Analysts say the vote will test whether his legacy can keep opposition supporters united.

Zambia's opposition is entering the 2026 general election without Edgar Lungu, the politician who for years united its biggest parties and inspired much of its support. Lungu, the country's former president, died in South Africa on June 5, 2025.

Opposition parties have since been competing to inherit his political legacy while trying to convince voters they remain a credible alternative to incumbent Hakainde Hichilema's ruling United Party for National Development (UPND).

Lungu had led the now dismantled Patriotic Front (PF) party, a faction of which became part of Zambia's overall opposition Tonse Alliance in 2024. The former president had also intitially been fronted as the coalition's 2026 presidential candidate.

Edgar Lungu was Zambia's president from 2015 to 2021 Image: Philippe Wojazer/Reuters/Pool/picture alliance

'The Edgar Lungu factor is still at play'

Political analyst Neo Simutanyi says Lungu's absence exposes an unresolved leadership question within the opposition coalition.

"He had a Plan B. He intended to back someone who would carry forward his political project, but he never had the opportunity to announce that person before he died," Simutanyi told DW.

Competing claims emerged over who should lead the Tonse Alliance emerged after Lungu's death. The coalition, now rebranded as the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance, has endorsed Brian Mundubile as its 2026 presidential candidate. He and Lungu were PF allies, while his running mate, Makebi Zulu, was Lungu's lawyer. Mundubile is widely seen as Hichilema's top challenger.

Simutanyi believes Lungu's influence nevertheless remains significant. "It is effectively a PF campaign without the PF label," he said, adding that several candidates are appealing to the same support base by presenting themselves as heirs to Lungu's legacy.

"The Edgar Lungu factor is still at play because candidates are campaigning on his legacy and many of the areas where he enjoyed strong support remain politically competitive."

Can Zambia's opposition deliver? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A battle for voters

Lungu's influence remains particularly visible on the Copperbelt, Zambia's mining heartland and one of the country's most competitive electoral battlegrounds.

"Edgar Lungu's absence has left a big vacuum in the opposition, especially in the Patriotic Front. He was the one holding the party together," said Agness Tembo, a young leader from the Copperbelt.

She warned that a fragmented opposition could weaken Zambia's competitive multiparty democracy. But not all voters believe personalities will decide the election.

Richard Mwamba, another Copperbelt resident, said many people are more concerned about their daily lives than political succession. "This election will be less about personalities and more about delivery — jobs, the cost of living, mining, electricity, roads and the prices of goods and services," he said.

Our time is now: Zambia's youth running in elections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For many PF supporters, however, Lungu's absence remains deeply felt. "Lungu united people from different political backgrounds. It will be difficult to find someone with the same influence," said supporter Mabvuto Phiri.

Tonse Pamodzi Alliance Secretary-General Celestine Mukandila rejects suggestions that the coalition has lost momentum. "President Lungu had once indicated that he had a Plan B. Today I can confirm that the Plan B is in place," Mukandila told DW. The alliance remains united behind Mundubile, he added.

"We are responding to president Lungu's call for unity of purpose and now have an opportunity to elect Brian Mundubile as president."

A regional test

Analysts say Zambia's opposition now faces a challenge seen elsewhere in Southern Africa, where parties have struggled after losing dominant leaders.

In Zimbabwe, opposition politics became increasingly fragmented following the death of Morgan Tsvangirai in 2018, while leadership transitions in other countries have also tested the ability of parties to remain united and electorally competitive.

Zambia has held regular multiparty elections since 1991 and is widely regarded as one of the region's more stable democracies. The election this year, analysts say, will show whether opposition parties can broaden their appeal beyond one influential political figure.

Lungu came to power in a special presidential election upon the death of then President Michael Sata in 2015. The following year, he was reelected to a five-year term. After losing power to Hichilema in a 2021 vote, Lungu returned to frontline politics and became the opposition's most influential leader.

Simutanyi says Lungu's political influence did not end with his death. His name may no longer appear on the ballot, but the contest over his legacy could still shape how many Zambians vote on August 13.

World.title: EU agrees to send border aid to Spain after Ceuta talks
World.content:
The Schengen Area was "in no way" compromised during the Ceuta incursion, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said after a video conference with his EU colleagues.

European Union interior ministers emerged from a video conference on Tuesday with an agreement to beef up external security, the group said in a statement.

"There was a common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight," they wrote in a press release.

Ministers also "pointed out that communication during moments of crisis could further be reinforced through timely coordination and should be more coherent, especially to counter malicious external actors engaged in foreign information manipulation and interference."

The group agreed to provide emergency aid to Spain to help boost border security.

Spain's Ceuta grapples with aftermath of border chaos To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What happened in Ceuta?

The meeting had been called to address concerns about security inside the Schengen free movement area after some 60,000 people rushed the border gates in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.

Hundreds among the group were minors, European NGOs have said.

The incident prompted a series of blistering critiques from center-right and right-wing leaders of EU member states against left-leaning Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez. Countries such as Italy and Finland called for an immediate suspension of Spain's membership in the Schengen agreement.

However, officials and law enforcement from across the EU have said that the breakdown of border controls was due to misinformation given to asylum seekers waiting on the border. Authorities also expressed suspicions that human trafficking gangs purposely misled the would-be migrants.

Spain's Ceuta exclave is located on the African continent, bordered by Morocco on one side and the sea on the other. It is subject to stricter-than-usual Schengen entry and exit procedures, as well as identity checks for passengers crossing over to the Spanish mainland.

Spain confirmed on Tuesday that some 60,000 people have returned to Morocco since the weekend, leaving 2,500 still in Ceuta.

What did EU interior ministers say?

"It is clear that in no way was the Schengen area compromised in this crisis," Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said after the talks with his counterparts in other EU nations.

His sentiment was echoed by French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez: "We all agreed the Schengen area was not really the problem."

European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner said that there was "full solidarity with Spain around the table" at the meeting. He added that increased border security provided by the EU's Frontex agency was already active in Ceuta and "ready to do more."

He called the meeting a "useful opportunity" to confirm that no one had moved from Ceuta to the mainland.

"These past few days were a test of our European resilience, a test of the security of our external borders," Brunner told. "Europe, I think, has definitely passed this test."

World.title: El Gobierno de Ayuso pagó 6,3 millones por el ático de Chamberí
World.content:
El ático de 485 metros cuadrados que el Gobierno de Isabel Díaz Ayuso (PP) compró hace tres meses a través de la empresa pública Planifica Madrid para usar como “oficinas” costó 6,3 millones de euros, según han confirmado a EL PAÍS dos fuentes cercanas a la operación. El piso, situado en el número 35 del paseo del General Martínez Campos y que la Comunidad de Madrid anunció que vendería día y medio después de que este periódico revelara la semana pasada la extraña compra, lo vendió una exclusiva inmobiliaria de lujo de La Moraleja que se llevó una comisión del 3%: 189.000 euros a cargo del vendedor.

La empresa pública Planifica Madrid, que depende de la consejería de Presidencia, adquirió el ático con una terraza de 200 metros cuadrados el 14 de abril y la operación no consta ni en el portal de transparencia, ni en las cuentas anuales de la compañía. Tampoco hay disponible para consulta una memoria justificativa ni una ampliación presupuestaria, como sí la ha habido para compras de otros inmuebles. De hecho, el precio final de la venta no había trascendido y las veces que se ha preguntado por ello a Ayuso, ha eludido la cuestión.

Promora, la inmobiliaria de lujo que intermedió en la venta y que está afincada en La Moraleja, publicó un anuncio con el ático a finales de enero y el precio de venta era de 6,6 millones. Finalmente, el apartamento costó 300.000 euros menos. Esta compañía se dedica al mercado de pisos y casas de lujo en toda la región y tuvo que firmar un acuerdo de confidencialidad y le pidieron “privacidad” y discreción durante toda la operación.

La decisión de canalizar la compra a través de Planifica Madrid también encareció la operación. A los 6,3 millones que costó el ático, hay que sumar otros 378.000 euros en concepto de Impuesto de Transmisiones Patrimoniales (ITP), tributo cedido a las comunidades autónomas.

Este último desembolso deriva de que la compra no la realizó directamente la Comunidad de Madrid, sino una sociedad mercantil de capital público. La legislación reconoce determinadas exenciones fiscales a la Administración autonómica, aunque esas exenciones no se aplican automáticamente a las sociedades mercantiles públicas que tributan con carácter general como cualquier otra sociedad, salvo previsión legal específica. Como el tributo se paga a la Comunidad, a nivel contable se abona el impuesto, pero en términos presupuestarios ese dinero vuelve a las arcas autonómicas.

Preguntada sobre por qué la compra se hizo a través de Planifica Madrid, una portavoz responde que la empresa pública “tiene por objeto la gestión del patrimonio inmobiliario de la Comunidad de Madrid” y que “está dentro de sus competencias de gestión patrimonial”.

En el anuncio publicado en las redes de Promora se describe el ático como un piso de “lujo absoluto”, con cinco habitaciones, seis baños y vistas panorámicas al skyline madrileño. También incluye montajes realizados con inteligencia artificial de cómo quedaría la casa si se quisiera utilizar como vivienda: un diseño del cuarto principal, del salón con salida a la terraza y de un hipotético despacho. “Diseño contemporáneo, domótica, dos plazas de garaje y dos trasteros. Privacidad, amplitud y una forma de vivir Madrid desde lo más alto”.

De la compra todavía hay varias incógnitas que ni la presidenta autonómica ni el consejero de Presidencia, Miguel Ángel García Martín, que también preside el consejo de administración de Planifica Madrid, han resuelto. “Todas las operaciones que realice esta empresa y cualquiera otra también estarán en sus memorias de actividades. Nosotros sí que rendimos cuentas, nosotros sí que somos transparentes”, dijo Martín durante una visita a la zona devastada por los incendios la semana pasada. Y fue él quien anunció, día y medio después de que este periódico destapara la adquisición del piso, que lo venderían junto con otros cuatro inmuebles en la Gran Vía para ayudar a la “reconstrucción” de la Sierra Oeste de Madrid, que quedó arrasada por el fuego. En total, esperan obtener entre 20 y 22 millones de euros, aseguró.

Denuncia ante el Tribunal de Cuentas

“Se eligió el camino más caro. También el menos visible. Nadie paga de más por casualidad”, opina el abogado Javier Flores, que ha interpuesto una denuncia ante el Tribunal de Cuentas para que investigue una posible responsabilidad contable por menoscabo de fondos públicos derivada de la compra y posterior venta del ático. Esto es, un supuesto perjuicio de los costes irreversibles derivados de adquirir y luego deshacerse de un inmueble que no ha llegado siquiera a usarse, como los gastos notariales y registrales o los honorarios a la inmobiliaria.

La operación se ha articulado por una vía que, a su juicio, es más costosa y menos garantista que el procedimiento ordinario. Cuando la Administración necesita un inmueble para uso público ―sería el caso del ático, según las explicaciones del Gobierno regional―, el procedimiento habitual pasa por la Dirección General de Patrimonio, que depende de la Consejería de Hacienda y exige la tramitación de un expediente administrativo completo. Ese expediente incluiría, entre otros, una propuesta razonada que justifique la necesidad de las nuevas dependencias y un informe de la propia Dirección General de Patrimonio, explica Flores por teléfono y alude a la ley de Patrimonio de la región.

Además, cuando la compra se hace de forma directa y por razones de urgencia, la legislación exige una autorización expresa del consejero de Hacienda y una motivación de las circunstancias excepcionales. Y la normativa, detalla el letrado, solo contempla este tipo de adquisiciones directas en supuestos muy concretos, como la existencia de una urgencia acreditada, la escasez de oferta en el mercado inmobiliario, la singularidad del inmueble o la necesidad de adquirir exactamente ese bien y no otro. “Sobre todo, se daría cuenta en el Parlamento Autonómico. De esto nos hemos enterado por la prensa, pero, en condiciones normales, lo habríamos sabido hace meses y en la Asamblea de Madrid todos los grupos habrían tenido la información”, concluye Flores.

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: NEC draw 0-0 at Olympiacos to boost Champions League hopes
World.content:
