The prime minister concludes his statement by asking why this “network of agents” did not display the same attitude towards Russia after the 2008 war, but only after the war in Ukraine began. Kobakhidze says society “will easily find a logical explanation” for that question.

“I believe there is a question that must be asked and carefully considered by society. We all know that, both in the past and today, this network of agents in Georgia has acted on instructions from external forces, and that its homeland is not Georgia but the ‘deep state’.

Against that backdrop, it is worth asking why they were not instructed to promote Russophobia when there was the strongest possible reason to do so – after the August 2008 war – and why they have been instructed to do so now, when the victim of Russian aggression is not their formal homeland but another country, albeit a friendly one. I believe society will easily find a logical explanation for this contradiction,” Kobakhidze wrote.

Kobakhidze on Russophobia in Georgia

World.title: Diaspora youth: Patriots or ‘information soldiers’? The hidden mission of camp in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan. More than 120 young people from 64 countries gathered in Zangilan under the slogan “Reviving Cities”. Officials told participants they should defend Azerbaijan’s achievements and push back against what they described as “biased campaigns”.

Against the backdrop of protesters calling Ilham Aliyev a “dictator” in Berlin, that message raises another question: is the state seeking to foster independent thinkers or “information soldiers” who will promote its official narrative abroad?

What was discussed at the 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp?

The 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp, which opened in Zangilan on 2 August, is officially presented as a platform for “patriotic education”, learning about “the realities on the ground” and rejuvenating the Azerbaijani diaspora. More than 120 young people from 64 countries are spending a week visiting reconstruction projects in the territories retaken by Azerbaijan, meeting government officials and learning what organisers describe as “Azerbaijani realities”.

A closer look at the speeches by Fuad Muradov, chairman of the State Committee for Work with the Diaspora, and other officials, however, reveals a more pragmatic objective. The government appears to see young people living abroad not simply as members of the diaspora with ties to their homeland, but as active participants in the information battle.

Muradov said the participants should be able to “respond with well-founded arguments to biased campaigns”. He said they should “represent” Azerbaijan’s interests with dignity in their countries of residence, on international platforms and within their own communities.

Another message struck an even tougher tone. Officials said that although their number was small, some people living abroad who called themselves Azerbaijanis did not welcome Azerbaijan’s successes. They urged participants to know who these people were, be familiar with their statements and respond to them with well-reasoned arguments. Officials also said “black PR”, “distortion of facts” and “organised campaigns” were unacceptable. At the same time, they said they remained open to “well-founded criticism”.

Elvin Aslanov, a representative of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, acknowledged that defending Azerbaijan abroad was “far from easy”, saying it required confronting double standards and disinformation. According to him, the young participants’ mission is to “convey the truth accurately and objectively”.

From the authorities’ perspective, such rhetoric may appear defensive and entirely legitimate. However, the broader context allows for another interpretation. Critics argue that the programme goes beyond patriotic education and instead systematically prepares “information soldiers” – young people expected to promote the official narrative on social media, in online discussions and in international debates. In other words, they see it as an attempt to build a state-directed “soft power” network.

What happened in Berlin, and why does it matter in this context?

The timing of these appeals is no coincidence. During Ilham Aliyev’s official visit to Germany on 21 July, Azerbaijani expatriates gathered on the streets of Berlin and chanted: “Dictator!”

Around the same time, Germany-based exiled blogger Alemdar Bunyatov approached Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev on a street in Berlin. He questioned them about political prisoners and allegations of torture.

Official media immediately described the incident as a “provocation” and portrayed Bunyatov as someone “known for his close ties to the Iranian intelligence services”. Responding to his questions, Bayramov dismissed the allegations of torture as “a personal opinion”.

Hajiyev, for his part, questioned Bunyatov about his sources of funding, his legal status in Germany and his reasons for leaving Azerbaijan. He stressed the importance of sovereignty and national security. The incident triggered a strong reaction in pro-government media, which portrayed the blogger’s questions as “provocative”.

The events in Berlin further illustrate the practical meaning of the messages delivered in Zangilan. In the official narrative, criticism is often framed as a “biased campaign”, “black PR” or the result of “external influence”.

As a result, the authorities themselves largely determine the line between “well-founded criticism” and a “biased campaign”. Young people, in turn, are expected to accept that distinction and challenge those whom the state places on the other side of it.

A method of training trolls?

Opposition figures and independent observers have long described such camps as a form of “troll factory”. Critics argue that their purpose is not to encourage independent thinking but to prepare young people to defend the official position on social media, in online discussions and before international audiences. They say that, under the banner of patriotism, organisers cultivate emotional attachment and ideological loyalty while encouraging participants to view critical voices as “hostile”.

Every country seeks to use its diaspora as a tool of soft power, and Azerbaijan is no exception. The problem, critics argue, is that the shrinking space for domestic criticism places a disproportionately heavy burden on young Azerbaijanis abroad to “defend” the official line. They must adapt to societies where freedom of expression is a fundamental principle while remaining loyal to Baku’s official narrative. For many young people, that contradiction can create genuine tension.

Muradov says, “We are open to dialogue”, while also insisting, “We will not tolerate black PR.” This raises an obvious question: what qualifies as “well-founded criticism”, and what counts as a “biased campaign”? If official media portray the questions and slogans heard on the streets of Berlin as a provocation, where is the line for young people who raise the same issues in international media or at academic forums?

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament holds first session as opposition, as expected, makes its presence felt
World.content:
First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

Armenia‘s newly elected parliament convened for the first time on 2 August. Three political forces won seats in the ninth National Assembly: the Civil Contract, Strong Armenia and Armenia factions. During the opening session, lawmakers managed only to appoint members of the Counting Commission. Heated exchanges between the ruling party and the opposition prevented them from addressing the rest of the agenda.

The opposition’s main grievance was the absence of the Catholicos from the opening session. The authorities did not invite him, and he did not bless the work of parliament. Opposition lawmakers described this as an unprecedented event in the history of independent Armenia.

Under the constitutional law governing the National Assembly’s rules of procedure, both the president and the Catholicos of All Armenians have the right to deliver opening remarks at parliament’s first session. This time, however, only President Vahagn Khachaturyan addressed lawmakers. Earlier, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said it had received no invitation for the Catholicos. When journalists asked Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan about Garegin II’s participation, he replied: “I do not know such a Catholicos.” The incident reflects the long-running dispute between the Armenian authorities and Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. More than two years ago, Prime Minister Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He initially argued that Garegin II could not lead the Armenian Apostolic Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and fathered a daughter. Pashinyan later accused him of links with foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party also included the removal of “the de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Lawmakers also fiercely debated the nomination of Ruben Rubinyan, the ruling party’s sole candidate for speaker of parliament.

Opposition MPs repeatedly referred to his research work at Istanbul Policy Center in Turkey in 2017–18. They asked whether he had interacted with local residents and even questioned what they looked like.

“Ask me directly whether I met representatives of the Turkish intelligence services in Turkey and whether they recruited me. Ask me: ‘Is that true?’ And I will answer: ‘No,'” Rubinyan said.

Parliament resumed its first session today. Lawmakers have already settled one of the main items on the agenda. In a secret ballot, they elected Ruben Rubinyan as speaker with 63 votes in favour and 28 against.

The opposition Armenia bloc boycotted the secret ballot. MPs from the second opposition force, the Strong Armenia faction, voted against Rubinyan’s nomination.

In the previous parliament, Rubinyan served as deputy speaker. Between 2022 and 2026, he also acted as Armenia’s special envoy for the normalisation of relations with Turkey. A few days ago, Rubinyan said he would be unable to continue in that role if parliament elected him speaker. The ruling party has not yet announced who will succeed him.

“Where is the Patriarch?” Opposition MPs visit him to receive his blessing

On the opening day of the session, opposition MPs began chanting, “Where is the Patriarch?” after the president’s address. During the oath-taking ceremony, they pointedly refused to stand or recite the oath. They said they were protesting the Catholicos’s absence. However, they signed the written text of the oath, allowing them to take office formally.

At the end of the first working day, MPs from both opposition factions visited the Catholicos’s residence.

The Mother See’s information service said Garegin II blessed the opposition lawmakers. He spoke of an “alarming situation and serious problems” facing the country. He also criticised what he described as the authorities’ “illegal and unconstitutional actions” against the Church.

Catholicos receives opposition MPs at the Mother See

The Catholicos praised what he described as the opposition MPs’ “devotion and filial love for the Church”. He said their stance was especially important at a time when “the authorities continue their campaign of repression, while national benefactor Samvel Karapetyan remains under arrest for speaking out in defence of Holy Etchmiadzin”.

In June last year, Armenian authorities opened a criminal case against Russian businessman and billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. Prosecutors accused him of publicly calling for the seizure and usurpation of power. In an interview with local media, Karapetyan discussed the escalating conflict between the government and the Church. He said he supported the Church and added: “If Armenia’s political forces fail to resolve this situation, we will have to intervene in the campaign against the Church in our own way.” His supporters founded the Strong Armenia party after his arrest, and he has remained under house arrest since December last year.

105 MPs in the new parliament

The three political forces that entered the National Assembly secured the following number of seats:

The ruling Civil Contract party – 64 seats

The Strong Armenia faction – 29 seats

The Armenia bloc – 12 seats

Strong Armenia leader and businessman Samvel Karapetyan did not enter parliament. During the election campaign, his allies confidently predicted victory and even said Karapetyan would become prime minister. However, he is ineligible to serve either as an MP or as prime minister. Under Armenia’s constitution, anyone holding citizenship of another country cannot hold either office. Karapetyan holds Armenian, Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

Former President Robert Kocharyan headed the electoral list of the Armenia bloc, making him its candidate for prime minister. However, Kocharyan declined to take up his parliamentary seat. His son, Levon Kocharyan, who also ran on the bloc’s list, accepted a mandate and has already joined parliament. He also served as an MP for the Armenia bloc in the previous legislature.

“I will do everything to ensure our children never experience war”

Rubinyan thanked the more than 700,000 voters who backed Civil Contract. He said they had given the ruling party “a mandate to continue Armenia’s democratic reforms and peace agenda”. According to Rubinyan, those voters had defended the country’s sovereignty and independence.

He said the time had come for Armenians to enjoy peaceful lives, have children and raise them without fear.

“My son, who is almost two years old, and children of his age have never experienced war. I will do everything to ensure that my children, your children and all our children never have to learn what war is,” he said.

Rubinyan also thanked those who voted for opposition parties out of conviction rather than in exchange for election bribes.

“It is time to change the political discourse,” Rubinyan says

Addressing opposition MPs, Rubinyan raised the issue of the tone of parliamentary debate. He said society, political circles and journalists had formed a common view of parliament in recent months. According to him, many now see the National Assembly as a place for pointless arguments, slander and insults.

“They say this parliament will be even worse than the previous one in that respect. It seems everyone expects exactly that from us. I want to propose that we break this curse together,” the speaker said.

He argued that the opposition factions had largely stayed away from the work of the previous, eighth convocation of parliament.

“All we saw here was political confrontation, shouting and radical speeches. It is time to change the narratives that have dominated Armenian politics over the past six years. I propose that we make this parliament a place for vigorous but respectful debate that never crosses the boundaries of decency.”

At the same time, he warned that if the opposition rejected his proposal and continued “down the well-trodden path”, the ruling party was ready to respond “in the toughest possible way”.

“Why did we take our seats?” Opposition MPs explain

Ishkhan Saghatelyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, argued that neither the opposition nor the ruling party had truly won the election.

He again claimed that the authorities had used administrative resources during the campaign and imprisoned opposition figures.

“This parliament has a serious legitimacy problem. We are here to organise political struggle and advance national goals. We are here to raise the concerns of Armenia’s citizens, speak about the prisoners held in Baku and Armenia’s occupied territories, and, yes, defend the people of Artsakh’s right to a collective return.”

Hayk Farmanyan, an MP from the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that message.

“We accepted our mandates to remain true to our Armenian identity, to fight for our national values, and to defend our dignity, our identity and our Church.”

Comment

Political analyst Lilit Dallakyan shared her impressions of the new parliament’s opening session on social media:

“Well, I ‘congratulate’ the Armenian people on the start of work by a new, high-quality, substantive parliament that is supposedly ready to tackle Armenia’s complex challenges.

The daily exchange of ‘Your father is a murderer’ [directed at MP Levon Kocharyan, son of former President Robert Kocharyan] will now gain a new, equally substantive argument: ‘Your uncle is a Russian oligarch’ [directed at MP Narek Karapetyan, nephew of Strong Armenia leader Samvel Karapetyan]. That will, in turn, prompt the reply: ‘You are Turkish dictators’ [directed at the authorities].

The only positive aspect is that this season of the series is unlikely to interest anyone or distract people from the real problems that are rapidly emerging.

At a time of profound change across the world, Armenian society and every individual will have to look for solutions to their own problems. Ultimately, that will bring about the changes the country needs.”

First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhaz diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive’
World.content:
Against the backdrop of the Pacific island nation of Nauru withdrawing its recognition of Abkhazia’s independence, prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania reflects on what Abkhazia’s foreign policy doctrine should look like.

Nauru, a small island nation in the Pacific region of Micronesia, recognised Abkhazia’s independence in 2009 but withdrew that recognition in late July 2026. The move reduced the number of countries recognising Abkhazia’s independence to four. Abkhazia’s foreign ministry said Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure”.

Akhra Bzhania said: “Around 230,000 irregular migrants crossed the EU’s borders in 2025–26 alone. All of them fled countries that enjoy broad international recognition.

Why didn’t they stay in Morocco, Mali or Afghanistan? Presumably because having a flag outside the UN headquarters does not automatically mean you live in a genuine state – one where you can influence public life, where your voice matters and where your dignity will never be trampled.

Being a recognised country and being a country where people want to live and are willing to die for it are two different things.

You may achieve the first and never attain the second. But if you have the second, then you have accomplished the most important task: building a country that belongs to its citizens. That is what defines a modern state. And that is precisely what should become the main instrument for Abkhazia’s integration into the international community.

Bzhania continued: “We must send a clear message to the international community that, despite sanctions, isolation and the threat of war, the people of Abkhazia have built a society based on the rule of law and freedom. Without being members of international institutions, we have incorporated the core principles of international conventions on civil and political rights into our system of governance.

We see ourselves as part of the international community and believe we deserve our rightful place within it. To achieve that, our diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive. It should focus not on waiting for or preserving acts of recognition, but on consistently demonstrating our statehood and expanding our international contacts.

No one else is obliged to do this for us. By recognising our sovereignty, Russia effectively made Abkhazia a subject of international law. But it cannot solve our problems on our behalf.”

Bzhania continued: “We must use every tool at our disposal to achieve our goals: the resources of the diaspora, cultural, trade and sporting ties, personal connections, migration policy and regional logistics. In this game, we need to keep raising the stakes.

Today, there is a window of opportunity for such an active policy. It is no secret that relations between Georgia and the West are at their lowest point since the 1990s. Those on whom Tbilisi relied to promote its anti-Abkhaz agenda have become disillusioned with Georgia, and we should take advantage of that. That includes reviving the active dialogue with European countries that existed in the late 1990s. After all, the hopes the West once placed in Georgia as a bastion of the free world in the Caucasus have, to a greater extent, been realised in Abkhazia.

Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: Beekeepers urge growers to add pollination services to their business plan
World.content:
The Australian horticulture industry has for generations relied on millions of feral honey bees to pollinate crops.

But as varroa mite spreads further north in Queensland, experts say free pollination from wild bee populations is disappearing, forcing growers to rethink how they produce food and secure commercial pollination services.

Bees provide essential pollination services in the horticulture industry. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

North Queensland commercial beekeeper Keith Lang said pollination services could no longer be taken for granted.

"People think bees are all about honey, but we can do without honey," he said.

"We can't do without pollination."

A hidden workforce

The Australian Honey Bee Industry Council says honey bees contribute about $4.6 billion in pollination services each year, helping produce about 65 horticultural crops across the country.

Chief executive Danny Le Feuvre said once varroa mite became established overseas, about 95 per cent of feral honey bee colonies disappeared.

Danny Le Feuvre says growers need to prepare for a reduction in feral bee populations. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

"For a long time, growers have benefited from free pollination from feral bees," he said.

"As those populations decline, growers will increasingly rely on managed hives supplied by commercial beekeepers."

The transition comes at a difficult time for the beekeeping industry.

Managing varroa mite has significantly increased costs and labour requirements, while low honey prices have made it harder for many businesses to remain profitable.

Mr Le Feuvre said surveys indicated a significant number of commercial beekeepers were considering leaving the industry just as demand for managed pollination services was expected to rise.

Test kits are used by commercial beekeepers such as Keith Lang to see if they have any varroa mite present in their hives. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

"We know we're going to need more colonies for pollination, but we're losing hives at exactly the same time," he said.

The industry has also released a new national Research, Development and Extension (RD & E) Plan, aimed at strengthening Australia's honey bee and pollination sector as it adapts to varroa mite.

The plan identifies priorities including improving varroa management, accelerating bee breeding and genetics, increasing pollination research, strengthening biosecurity and supporting commercial beekeepers to maintain healthy hive numbers for both honey production and crop pollination.

Beekeepers are struggling to meet demand for hives during pollination season. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Growers face rising costs

Bundaberg horticultural agronomist and avocado grower Lisa Fyffe knows first-hand how important pollination is for production.

"The European honey bee is definitely the most effective pollinator we have," she said.

"If varroa takes out those wild populations, what do we do then? All of a sudden the reliance on commercial beekeepers increases, and I don't think anyone is really ready for it."

Lisa Fyffe says growers need to work with beekeepers to manage pollination of their crops. (Supplied)

Ms Fyffe said pollination costs had already increased significantly.

"The price has doubled per hive," she said.

"A $50,000 pollination bill suddenly becomes a $100,000 bill. If you don't have the fruit set in the first place, you don't have a crop to sell."

She said growers also needed to rethink how they managed their orchards by providing better habitat for pollinators through flowering ground cover, water sources and improved biodiversity.

"It's so much bigger than what we think," she said.

Planning ahead

The National Farmers' Federation Horticulture Council is encouraging growers to start planning earlier for pollination services rather than waiting until flowering begins.

Executive officer Richard Shannon said growers needed to start treating pollination as an essential business input and incorporate it into their seasonal planning.

Richard Shannon says the costs need to be fairly shared between producers, corporates and consumers. (ABC News: Nathan Morris)

"The purpose is to help growers understand what their future pollination needs might be and encourage them to start those conversations with beekeepers much earlier," he said.

Communication will be critical

Both the horticulture and beekeeping industries agree stronger communication between growers and commercial beekeepers will be essential as Australia continues to adapt to living with varroa mite.

Mr Le Feuvre said early planning was imperative to avoid competition in securing healthy hives for pollination.

He also urged Australians to support local beekeepers by purchasing Australian honey.

"The best way we're going to get through this is by improving profitability for our beekeepers so they can rebuild hive numbers and continue supplying pollination services," he said.

Beekeepers hope their hives are able to survive the varroa mite incursion. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

As the free pollination once provided by feral bees disappears, Keith Lang said commercial beekeepers would carry more of the responsibility for keeping crops productive.

"It's not just beekeepers; it's the farmers as well that's going to be hit," he said.

World.title: Smith says he will '100 per cent' return to PGA Tour if LIV Golf fails
World.content:
Cameron Smith wants LIV Golf to survive, but if it does not, he would "100 per cent" return to the PGA Tour.

"I mean, if it was the only option, I think that's where everyone would want to be for sure, 100 per cent," the Australian and former World No.2 told reporters ahead of this week's LIV Golf New York event. "It would go back to old times."

But Smith made it clear he would strongly prefer that the current times with LIV Golf can continue.

"I want it to work, really, to be honest. It's great fun out here. The team that we've got, I feel like we make each other better, better people and better golfers as well," Smith said. "Yeah, I'd hate to see it go away. We'll see what happens."

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced in April that it will not continue its financial support of the league beyond this season. Smith signed with the breakaway league in 2022, receiving a contract reportedly worth $US140 million ($198.72 million).

Smith is the captain of the all-Australian team Ripper GC.

"What we've been able to do for golf in Australia is really quite important to me, junior golf, the Little Rippers, the event that we have down there, the people it brings out to showcase our great league," Smith said.

"It would be a shame for all that to go away, and I feel like we've worked really hard over the last three or four years to kind of make that all happen."

LIV Golf's Adelaide event in February was among the league's most popular stops this season and set records for golf in Australia. More than 115,000 fans attended across the week in Adelaide, making it the highest-attended golf event in the country's history.

"Australian golf is important to me. I think [LIV] improves it," Smith said.

"I think all the numbers are up. The memberships are up. Social play is up. I think that's in part because of us. So I think it would be a shame for Australian golf if it did go away."

Though multiple reports say the LIV Golf Team Championship scheduled for late August in Michigan will be cancelled amid the league's financial troubles, the players have reportedly been told to prepare as if it is on schedule, and Smith said he's doing just that.

"We had a great year there last year in Detroit, and we're hoping we get back there," he said of the season-ending event from August 27 to 30 at The Cardinal at Saint John's Resort in Plymouth, Michigan.

"It's a great golf course, a great venue, and the crowds really turned up as well. Yeah, would be disappointed if it wasn't."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

LIV Golf has been mum on the status of the $40 million event, which has $11.2 million going to the winning team. However, The Cardinal, which hosted the 2025 LIV team championship, has no tournament infrastructure or fan hospitality built out yet, Front Office Sports reported last week.

Smith said the LIV team is working hard "behind the scenes" to get them playing next year, and he hopes to learn more at an upcoming players' meeting.

"I don't really understand what is going to happen. I think it's all up in the air," he said. "I feel like we're well-informed, but I feel like a lot of it is still up in the air. We don't know."

When asked about his plans if LIV Golf folds, he said he has not made any.

"I'm contracted to the end of next year, so I was expecting to play until the end of next year and renegotiate and hopefully go on," Smith said.

"I'm a positive guy, so I've made no effort to go seek anything else."

Reuters

World.title: WA government has no plans to change uranium mining ban
World.content:
The West Australian government will maintain its ban on uranium mining, despite growing global demand and a landmark export deal with India.

The state's uranium policy, in place since Labor's election in 2017, allowed projects approved by the previous Liberal-National government to proceed, but banned all others.

None of those projects have reached production, with Deep Yellow's Mulga Rock, around 850 kilometres north-east of Perth, the only one still meeting the government's criteria.

Newly sworn-in Mines Minister Daniel Pastorelli has ruled out any change ahead of his first appearance at Kalgoorlie's Diggers and Dealers Mining Forum today.

It leaves South Australia as the only state actively producing and exporting uranium.

Deep Yellow's Mulga Rock uranium mine, pictured here in concept art, is the only project allowed to proceed under current WA government policy. (Supplied: Deep Yellow)

"Uranium mining is banned in Western Australia and the state government has no plans to change its existing policy," a spokesperson said.

"We know Western Australia will be a global renewable energy powerhouse into the future, and we must do everything we can to bring that industry alive."

The combination of domestic political opposition and a uranium price that fell as low as $US21/pound in the wake of the 2011 Fukushima Nuclear disaster has made for a difficult road for would be Australian miners.

Conservation groups maintain the potential environmental impact outweighs any economic benefit.

But growing global demand, including the deal with the Modi government signed last month allowing uranium exports to India for the first time, have left the industry hopeful for change in WA.

Marnie Finlayson is managing director of DevEx Resources, which is exploring for uranium in the Northern Territory. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Marnie Finlayson is managing director of DevEX Resources, which is exploring for uranium in the Northern Territory, and was one of only two female presenters at this year's Diggers and Dealers.

She said uranium mining will support jobs and economic growth.

"I do believe it will happen over time, and I think there has to be a growing emphasis on what it brings to those states that don't currently allow it," she said.

"There needs to be a more concerted effort around changing the sentiment around uranium mining and the benefits it will bring to those states."

'Would be welcome': High commissioner

Indian high commissioner to Australia Nagesh Singh said he would welcome a decision by the WA government to lift its ban on uranium mining.

"For us, we would like to see more and more supply … I am told by some experts that India is going to be perhaps the biggest market for uranium supplies," he said during a visit to Kalgoorlie last week.

"Of course, I can't dictate terms to the Australian government or the West Australian government, it's for them to decide, but it will be a very welcome step as far as we're concerned."

India's high commissioner to Australia, Nagesh Singh, with WA School of Mines student Amol Chaudhari and the Minerals Council of Australia's David Parker. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Western Australia's opposition has pledged to overturn the ban if elected in future.

But Australia's peak mining exploration body said the debate needed to shift beyond politics.

"We're still stuck on local politics," Association of Mining and Exploration Companies chief executive Warren Pearce said.

"We've got to get past that and recognise this can be done safely every day in Australia.

"There's no reason we shouldn't be doing this in WA, there's no reason we shouldn't be doing this in Queensland and there's lots of countries that need our support."

Significant opportunity

WA Chamber of Minerals and Energy chief executive Aaron Morey said uranium prices, which hit $US85/pound in June, had reached a point where mining in WA would be economically feasible.

"The price increases we have seen are sustainable," Mr Morey said.

"There has been a material increase in demand that will persist into the future, due to the renewed interest in nuclear energy, because it is clean, it is efficient, and it is reliable."

Aaron Morey says there is no reason why WA cannot mine the uranium needed for other countries. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

He said the resource represented a significant opportunity for WA.

"Other countries around the world aren't as blessed as we are with our renewable resources, and so for many countries, nuclear and uranium as an input is absolutely vital to their future," Mr Morey says.

"We do have world class deposits here in Western Australia, there is significant commercial interest in developing those deposits, and so we continue to work with the government to ensure they can proceed."

World.title: 'The world must see': Zelenskyy shares video of drone hunting down vegetable seller
World.content:
Ukraine has accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson.

Footage released by Ukrainian police and shared online by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shows the drone pursuing a man around a van being used as a street stand, before diving towards him and exploding as he ducks for cover behind the vehicle.

The 52-year-old man, who was identified only as Yurii, survived but suffered shock and shrapnel injuries, according to Ukrainian officials.

"Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone 'safari' Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson," Mr Zelenskyy wrote on X as he shared the video.

"The world must see this. It must see every piece of evidence that Russia has gone mad and that its soldiers take pleasure in killing and abusing civilians.

"Without pressure on Russia, the dismantling of its capacity for aggression, and real security guarantees, it is simply impossible to imagine the world being able to coexist with this evil."

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy surveys the aftermath of a Russian strike in Kyiv last month. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

The location of the video was verified by the Reuters news agency, using the road layout and vegetation that matched satellite and archive imagery.

The date of the attack could not be independently confirmed, but Ukrainian police and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident happened on Tuesday.

Russia's Defence Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

'There is nowhere to go. It is terrifying'

Yurii, the vegetable seller, had travelled to Kherson on the morning of the attack to sell produce, according to Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration.

Ukrainian officials later released a video of him being interviewed as he sat on a bed in a hospital ward.

"I only just put up the umbrella and started unloading the boxes. My wife was there, too," Yurii says in the video.

"Then we heard it buzzing, but could not even see it. It came from somewhere behind the market, from those bushes over there, and flew in very low.

"It is open steppe. There is nowhere to go. It is terrifying, of course. Really terrifying."

In the video, Yurii shows that he is wounded on both legs and also on his back. His wife ran off and was not injured, he said.

The foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the attack formed part of a deliberate Russian campaign to intimidate civilians.

"This barbaric Russian war crime in Kherson demands international condemnation and justice, but thousands of similar crimes never come to the public eye," he wrote on Telegram.

Civilian casualties on the rise, UN says

In July, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said it had documented 1,396 civilian deaths and 7,978 injuries in the first six months of 2026, marking a 37 per cent increase from 2025 and more than double the figures from 2024.

Five dead in Moscow region as Kyiv targets more Wildberries sites Ukraine also targeted another warehouse belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries, as both sides traded strikes.

It said that the surge in civilian casualties was primarily driven by intensifying Russian long-range missile and drone strikes targeting cities far from the front lines.

Ukraine is also attacking Russia with drones and long-range missiles, many of which have caused civilian casualties, Russian authorities say.

Russia on Monday accused Ukraine of terrorism after seven people, including three children, were killed at the Black Sea holiday resort of Gelendzhik, in what it said was a deliberate Ukrainian drone attack on civilians.

A Ukrainian official said that the drone only fell on the beach in Gelendzhik because it was shot down by Russian air defences, adding that "Ukraine uses its weapons exclusively against the Russian military-industrial complex and economic infrastructure facilities".

Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians in the war, which was triggered by Russia's ⁠invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Jetstar to charge new fees for overhead carry-on baggage
World.content:
Jetstar has announced it will charge passengers to stow carry-on luggage in overhead lockers from next year, allowing only a small under-seat bag at no extra cost.

The budget airline is set to scrap its free 7 kilogram carry-on allowance from February 2027, in a move it says is in line with other low-fare carriers globally.

The changes will see all bookings allow one small bag such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag to be stored under the seat, while extra carry-on luggage will cost at least $25 per flight.

In a statement, Jetstar said feedback had shown that having bags weighed at the gate and struggling to find room in overhead lockers were "the more stressful parts of the airport experience".

Jetstar said it will ask customers to keep carry-on bags under 10kg so they can safely lift it themselves. (Supplied: Jetstar)

"We know that weighing carry-on bags at the gate can be frustrating for our customers and for our crew," Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully said.

Ms Tully said the changes would allow for better use of overhead locker space, streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time.

"Our new carry-on baggage model provides more choice to customers while helping to keep our fares low," she said.

"You only pay for what you need — travelling with less means paying less, and you can always add more if you need."

From February 2 next year, overhead carry-on luggage will not be weighed but will be restricted to bags measuring 56x36x23cm.

The cost will start at $25 per domestic one-way flight, while the add-on could be an extra $52 for an international flight between Cairns and Tokyo, according to a list of examples provided.

Loading...

Under-seat baggage allowance included in every fare will be restricted to one bag measuring 40×30×20cm.

There are no changes to Jetstar's checked baggage fees, which remain purchasable for up to 40kg per passenger.

The airline's statement said customers with existing bookings after February 2, 2027, will be upgraded to include priority carry-on at no cost.

Independent senator David Pocock said if Jetstar wanted to improve its on-time performance it should "just do that, not blame customers".

"Seems like you have to check yourself on these days, do everything yourself, and then get charged for everything," he told ABC News Breakfast.

"We've seen so little action from the government to hold airlines to account. In an airline industry where we know there's not much choice, there's not much competition.

"I think there's a real role for regulation and actually ensuring that Australians get better service."

World.title: Motorcycle rider critical after Townsville garbage truck crash
World.content:
A motorcyclist has suffered life-threatening injuries after a collision with a council rubbish truck in Townsville.

The crash at Webb Drive in Mount St John was reported to emergency services at 5:51am.

A Queensland Ambulance Service spokesperson said the male motorcycle rider had suffered critical injuries.

A spokesperson for the council said the local government was working closely with Queensland Police, who were investigating the incident.

"As a result, Webb Drive is expected to remain closed for approximately three hours," the spokesperson said.

Road closures are causing some traffic delays as police investigate the crash. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Townsville Mayor Nick Dametto said the truck involved in the collision had recently left a council depot.

"As people might know, our waste trucks are actually stored down at the end of Webb Drive and one of the first trucks coming out this morning was involved in this," he said.

Councillor Dametto said no rubbish would be collected by council on Wednesday.

The crash follows a fatal collision between a Townsville City Council garbage truck and a pedestrian in July 2025.

An 85-year-old woman died as a result of the incident, which happened at a residential street in Bushland Beach.

World.title: Calls to permanently open historic tunnel in Sydney's Blue Mountains
World.content:
Blue Mountains City Council wants $15 million to permanently reopen a 134-year-old tunnel that drew sell-out crowds at the weekend.

Originally built for a railway to the mountains in 1892, the Lapstone Hill Tunnel once stored munitions and mustard gas during World War II and at one point served as a mushroom farm.

Mayor Mark Greenhill says council spent $4 million from a state government grant to clean out the tunnel and install lighting.

Council want to open the tunnel permanently as a tourist attrtaction and walking route. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

However, he says further funding is needed to build car parking and easy access and exit to the site.

"What we're seeking is partnership from the other levels of government so that this really amazing piece of Australia's history can be opened up permanently," Cr Greenhill said.

" It is like walking back in time to another era. "

Cr Greenhill says the council has a temporary lease on the state-owned site which is due to end by the end of the year.

The Lapstone Hill Tunnel was originally conceived as a railway tunnel through the Lapstone monocline. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

"My fear is this, if we don't get some funding by the end of the year, the license will finish. All the work we've done will be for naught," Cr Greenhill said.

"All the work we've done to clean it up, put lights in it, it'll have been for nothing and might be locked away for another couple of centuries."

The council argues opening the tunnel would provide a safer cycling route between Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains, potentially removing cyclists from the Great Western Highway between Glenbrook and Lapstone.

The state heritage-listed tunnel was opened in 1892 as a railway tunnel in the Blue Mountains, but was later closed in 1913 because it was too steep for trains.

Lapstone local David Watson says the tunnel represents a "missing link" for cyclists. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

Locals back permanent opening

Thousands of residents and visitors attended open days over the last two weekends, which allowed for walk-throughs of the historic tunnel.

David Watson grew up in Lapstone and remembers the tunnel portals being a scary place because they were locked up and inaccessible.

He started campaigning to open the tunnel in 2012 after seeing the portals surrounded by disused shipping containers and forklifts from its days as a mushroom farm.

""This would be a perfect thing for people to walk through with their dogs or their kids and for push bikes to ride through," Mr Watson said.

" This is like a missing link that would … get cyclists off the busy highway but also get walkers back into the lower mountains. "

Lapstone local Michele Corin said the tunnel was inspiring a sense of wonder in Blue Mountains residents who turned up in droves.

"It's a place that brings people together, strengthens local identity and showcases the heritage that shaped our region," Ms Corin said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure said the state government would support the council's efforts to activate the site "while pursuing alternate funding sources".

"The NSW Government previously provided $4 million to Blue Mountains City Council for remediation of the Lapstone Tunnel," the spokesperson said.

World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars Stan Choe Updated August 5, 2026 — 6:50am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market rallied to records as companies kept piling up profits and oil prices eased. The S&P 500 shot up 1.8 per cent, and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set in June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.7 per cent to its own record set the day before, and the Nasdaq composite jumped 2.6 per cent. Palantir Technologies and Caterpillar helped lead the way after becoming the latest companies to deliver stronger profits for the spring than expected. Wall Street is roaring higher as a raft of companies deliver better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.01am AEST pointing to a gain of 35 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX jumped 1.4 per cent to a record high on Tuesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US70.47¢. SpaceX reported a loss of $US541 million ($767.8 million) in its first quarterly report as a public company, but the loss was less than Wall Street expected and revenue soared.



The company run by Elon Musk, or 9 cents per share, in the three months through June, less than half what financial analysts had expected. Revenue jumped to $US7.8 billion, up more than 90 per cent from the year-earlier period. Despite worries about high inflation, the war in Iran and a possible bubble in stock prices because of euphoria around the boom in artificial-intelligence technology, Wall Street is nearing its latest apex in large part because profits are soaring for companies. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term. Related Article Opinion

Currencies The real reason Trump just rushed to help Japan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Palantir Technologies helped lead the way and soared 29.5 per cent after CEO Alex Karp said its overall revenue leaped 93 per cent in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Besides reporting a stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected, the AI company also raised its revenue forecast for the full year of 2026. Caterpillar climbed 5.5 per cent after the heavy-equipment maker likewise reported stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. It was the first time Caterpillar made more than $US20 billion ($28.4 billion) in sales and revenue in a quarter, and CEO Joe Creed said it’s seeing strong order rates and a growing backlog across its main businesses.



Caterpillar is also benefiting from the AI boom through increased orders for turbines used to power data centres, among other things. They’re the latest companies to deliver even better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected, following strong results from Amazon, Microsoft and others. Coming into this week, companies in the S&P 500 index were on track to deliver growth of nearly 50 per cent in earnings per share for the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That would be the biggest such jump since 2021, when the economy was roaring back to life after cratering in the COVID-19 pandemic. With corporate profits up so much, while stock prices are still roughly where they were two months ago, stocks don’t look as expensive as they did before, according to Phil Segner, a co-portfolio manager at the Leuthold Group. Also helping stocks on Tuesday was another drop for oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, sank 5.4 per cent to $US79.25 per barrel as hope once again took over from fear in the oil market. It had swung sharply between $US72 and $US102 through July on uncertainty about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude around the world.



It’s jerked up and down many times as uncertainty built, receded and then built again, not only week to week but also hour to hour. Analysts warned more swings could still be ahead, but the latest drop in oil prices nevertheless helped to ease Wall Street’s worries about inflation. That in turn pulled down yields in the bond market, which relaxes pressure on the overall economy and on prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.63 per cent from 4.70 per cent Monday and from 4.75 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Higher yields make it more expensive for all kinds of Americans to borrow money, from homebuyers looking for a mortgage to big companies looking to build AI data centres. Related Article Opinion

Appliances He lied about an affair and cost his company nearly $30 million. Now he has a new job Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Reports on the US economy, meanwhile, showed it remains resilient even though inflation remains worse than anyone would like. One said US employers were advertising nearly 7.4 million job openings at the end of June, a slight slowdown from May’s level but close to economists’ expectations.



In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi had a more significant move and rose 1.6 per cent. Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings recently because its stock market is dominated by two companies swept up in AI mania, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The Kospi had dropped 5.1 per cent and soared 17.9 per cent in the prior two days. Stocks of computer chip companies also strengthened on Wall Street, where gains of 2.5 per cent for Nvidia, 6.6 per cent for Broadcom and 7.6 per cent for Micron Technology were some of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. World.title: ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack David Crowe August 5, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A man selling vegetables in a Ukrainian town survived an attack by a Russian drone after it chased him around his vehicle in a chilling strike captured on video and shared around the world. The attack drew condemnation as an example of a “human safari” by Russian drone operators who watch for civilians and follow them with their airborne explosives in the manner of a computer game. Loading Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the attack as a crime and said the man under attack in the southern city of Kherson had been wounded in the blast. “A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him,” he said.



“Every single day, ordinary people in Kherson face these Russian ‘safaris’.” Kherson, located across the Dnipro River from Russian forces, has seen hundreds of drone attacks on civilians over the past year, leading local authorities to install netting and other barriers to try to protect citizens. Many of the city’s most important functions have been moved underground to escape the attacks, which became so commonplace that Ukrainians coined the term “human safari” for the Russian tactics. Warning: Graphic content View post on X



The drones are fitted with cameras to allow a “first-person view” by the Russian operator, who can look for a target, even if it is a civilian on a city street. The horrific video highlighted the scale of this threat by showing how the vegetable seller tried to hide from the drone as it hovered around his van. The man was identified as Yurii, 52, who came to Kherson from a nearby area to sell fresh produce, according to the Kyiv Independent and other Ukrainian media. The video shows him trying to dodge the drone, which hovers around and over the van, before the device detonates near him. He was taken to hospital suffering from shrapnel wounds and concussion. In a video released by the local military officials, Yurii said he was trying to show the drone operator that he was only selling vegetables. “But it started flying right at me,” he added. He said his wife was able to escape.



Drone operator is a ‘sadist’ Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the attack a “barbaric” Russian war crime and said thousands of similar attacks never reached the public eye. “This is a deliberate and systemic Russian strategy. They know exactly what they are doing. The sadist operating this drone knows full well that he is targeting a civilian,” he said. Drones have increased in speed and range to the point where the danger zone for soldiers and civilians can extend for 25 kilometres on either side of the front line, according to Ukrainian military officials. This “kill zone” is wide enough to include entire cities such as Kherson. When The New York Times reported on the “safaris” in January, local officials said about 200 civilians had been killed and 2000 wounded in the drone strikes over the past year.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war How dodging drones and death became daily life in eastern Ukraine In May, Ukrainian soldiers in Kherson told a reporter from London’s The Telegraph of the way they hacked into the feeds of the FPV drones to see the vision being relayed to a Russian operator, helping them identify the threats and destroy them. “On a busy day, we might shoot down ten drones,” the operator of the drone detection equipment told the newspaper. One Ukrainian aid worker recently told this masthead of a narrow escape from an FPV drone near a village outside Kharkiv, another city close to Russian forces. “There was an FPV drone just flying after our car, and I was terrified,” said Anastasiia Bilchenko. “We could see, from our drone detector, that the eyes of the drone were following us.”



The Kherson attack came one day after the widespread circulation of a video showing a Ukrainian drone falling on a Russian beach at a Black Sea resort crowded with civilians. Russian officials said seven people died, including three children, and another 58 were injured. Loading The video showed the drone falling at Gelendzhik, east of Crimea, and exploding on the beach. Russian authorities accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, while Ukrainian official Andriy Kovalenko said the drone had been shot down by Russian air defence personnel. World.title: My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingAsk an expert Opinion My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start? Noel Whittaker Money columnist August 5, 2026 — 5:01am

August 5, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

My children, aged 10 and 13, would like to start investing a modest amount in shares. They will have about $4000 to start and may then top up their investment once or twice a year with birthday, Christmas and pocket money. Could you please outline the best options in terms of simplicity and tax treatment, both now and into the future? I’m not sure whether the shares should be held in my name or theirs. My gross income is about $104,000 and my husband’s is $182,700. We don’t want to spend too much time establishing or maintaining the investment – we’re looking for a “set and forget” approach – but we do want to be able to easily see fees, tax, performance (gains or losses) and overall returns. I’ve heard that platforms such as CommSec and Vanguard are fairly simple. Helping your kids invest their hard-earned can put them well ahead in life. Simon Letch. It’s terrific that your children want to start investing while they’re still so young. Time is the greatest asset an investor has, and starting early can make an enormous difference to the wealth they build over their lifetime. One option is to buy shares or exchange-traded funds (ETFs) through a platform such as CommSec or Vanguard. But before you do that, think carefully about who should own the investment.



If the shares are held in a child’s name, special tax rules apply and investment income above modest limits is generally taxed at penalty rates. If they’re held in a parent’s name, those rules don’t apply, but all income and capital gains are taxed at the parent’s marginal tax rate. There is another option that deserves serious consideration: an investment bond. It’s one of the simplest long-term investments available and ideal for a “set and forget” strategy. The recent changes rushed through Parliament have changed the rules dramatically. World.title: Can’t afford a house on your own? This could be the solution
World.content:
MoneyTaxProperty investment Can’t afford a house on your own? This could be the solution Caterina Hrysomallis August 5, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to living with friends, Australians are no strangers, with many of us living in sharehouses in our 20s and 30s. But would you ever take it beyond just renting? A 2024 survey found that over half of Australians would consider buying a property with a friend or sibling. However, only 4 per cent of respondents in the same survey had actually done so. Who says someone should live alone if they don’t want to, just because they’re single? Steven Siewert Current data might reflect otherwise. Deanna Lastrina, senior property lawyer at Nest Legal says, “I’ve had far more enquiries coming in for co-ownership agreements, particularly in the last eight months”. People are wanting “accelerated access into the market, which is particularly hard for first home buyers without parental assistance”.



“You might have lived or grown up in a particular postcode, and perhaps you don’t want to exit that postcode. But by pulling those resources together, you could still live in those ‘untouchable’ areas,” she says. Another big factor? The power of companionship, especially in a post-COVID world. Who says someone should live alone if they don’t want to, just because they’re single? I absolutely believe all friends buying property together should have legal documents drawn up. Deanna Lastrina, senior property lawyer at Nest Legal Karli* and Mark* are a success story. They’re friends who had been renting together for a few years. When they started looking at buying their own homes, Karli realised that if she wanted to stay in a similar area, her budget might only have got her a tiny apartment. The friends started exploring the idea of buying a home together. Four auctions later, they bought a house in May 2024. They’ve been living in the property since.



They’re tenants in common, meaning they have distinct shares in the property and can sell or bequeath as they wish. These shares can be even or uneven. Editor's pick First home buyers I bought a house in my 20s with a friend, and we’re still friends The other structure is a joint tenancy, which involves 50/50 ownership and the “right of survivorship”, meaning if one owner dies, the other automatically inherits the entire property. For friends, Lastrina strongly recommends a tenants in common structure. “Our agreement was a 50/50 split, even if someone else had more money as a deposit,” Karli says. Maintenance and repairs are split 50/50, too. “We did our own research into different banks, as we wanted a loan each and individual offset accounts. Only two banks offered this kind of loan, at the time.” It’s going so well, they’re considering buying an investment property in a regional area.



Lastrina spotlights two big considerations when it comes to these arrangements. “The first is choosing the right person to live with. It goes beyond someone you get along with. They need to be someone that you consider financially disciplined. Someone you’ll be able to resolve conflict with, swiftly.” The second? “I absolutely believe all friends buying property together should have legal documents drawn up.” A “co-ownership agreement” can outline: How much each person initially contributed to the property

How mortgage repayments and bills are paid

How renovations, repayment defaults and disputes are treated

What happens if one owner wants to sell

And what happens if one owner loses decision-making capacity or dies Buyers should also investigate whether they need estate planning and/or family law advice, and to do so at the outset, before the property purchase. One of the biggest mistakes people make is failing to consider worst-case scenarios.



Lastrina recalls one case where two friends bought a property and one sadly passed away. The deceased’s share of the property was passed on to their younger sibling, as per their will. Editor's pick Opinion

Property investment Why Australians can no longer count on property to make them rich “The surviving owner now owns a property with a friend’s younger sibling, a person they don’t really know or trust. Because there was no co-ownership agreement in place, there was no mechanism that meant the surviving owner could easily purchase half of the property.” These agreements aren’t solely about mitigating scenarios as serious. There can be fun clauses, too. “One of my favourite clauses is that every six weeks, the parties have a meeting – almost like an AGM.” Karli and Mark were both single when they bought, which raises the million-dollar question: what happens if one of them enters a relationship?



“Ideally, the plan would be to rent the property out rather than add a third person into the considerations.” They’ve decided to discuss this further if the time comes and re-engage a lawyer. Lastrina says that people can stipulate what happens if an owner finds a partner in a co-ownership agreement. If this does happen, she recommends the couple sets up a binding financial agreement (Australia’s version of a prenup) giving them more certainty around how their respective interests would be dealt with if they separated, which can indirectly benefit co-owners by providing greater clarity in the event of relationship breakdowns. *These names have been changed. World.title: Think soup is boring? These bowls bring colour, crunch and main meal energy
World.content:
From halloumi fries to crispy-skinned chicken, these hearty soups have the satisfying texture already built in. No side of bread required.

I love soup. But I know sceptics exist. To them, soup isn’t a meal unless it’s accompanied by a cheese-oozing toastie or a slab of sourdough the size of a world atlas.

Honestly? I respect that kind of aggressive dedication to dinner. But to save you the side-dish admin, I’ve skipped straight to the chase. Here are soups with the something-something already built in. We’re talking halloumi fries, dunkable spring rolls and hunks of gloriously crispy-skinned chicken. No sides required.

Halloumi “fries” launch zaatar-roasted tomato soup into a new flavour realm. Katrina Meynink

Zaatar-roasted tomato soup with halloumi fries

In culinary school, a German chef once admonished my “thick soup”, going on a tirade about Australians and our horrifying love for a dense puree. Consider me a proud, card-carrying thick-soup advocate until the end of my days. How else could a bowl carry the piping hot, salty squeak of tanned halloumi fries? It takes a standard tomato soup and pushes it into an entirely new realm of mealtime.

World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars Stan Choe Updated August 5, 2026 — 6:50am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market rallied to records as companies kept piling up profits and oil prices eased. The S&P 500 shot up 1.8 per cent, and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set in June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.7 per cent to its own record set the day before, and the Nasdaq composite jumped 2.6 per cent. Palantir Technologies and Caterpillar helped lead the way after becoming the latest companies to deliver stronger profits for the spring than expected. Wall Street is roaring higher as a raft of companies deliver better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.01am AEST pointing to a gain of 35 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX jumped 1.4 per cent to a record high on Tuesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US70.47¢. SpaceX reported a loss of $US541 million ($767.8 million) in its first quarterly report as a public company, but the loss was less than Wall Street expected and revenue soared.



The company run by Elon Musk, or 9 cents per share, in the three months through June, less than half what financial analysts had expected. Revenue jumped to $US7.8 billion, up more than 90 per cent from the year-earlier period. Despite worries about high inflation, the war in Iran and a possible bubble in stock prices because of euphoria around the boom in artificial-intelligence technology, Wall Street is nearing its latest apex in large part because profits are soaring for companies. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term. Related Article Opinion

Currencies The real reason Trump just rushed to help Japan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Palantir Technologies helped lead the way and soared 29.5 per cent after CEO Alex Karp said its overall revenue leaped 93 per cent in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Besides reporting a stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected, the AI company also raised its revenue forecast for the full year of 2026. Caterpillar climbed 5.5 per cent after the heavy-equipment maker likewise reported stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. It was the first time Caterpillar made more than $US20 billion ($28.4 billion) in sales and revenue in a quarter, and CEO Joe Creed said it’s seeing strong order rates and a growing backlog across its main businesses.



Caterpillar is also benefiting from the AI boom through increased orders for turbines used to power data centres, among other things. They’re the latest companies to deliver even better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected, following strong results from Amazon, Microsoft and others. Coming into this week, companies in the S&P 500 index were on track to deliver growth of nearly 50 per cent in earnings per share for the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That would be the biggest such jump since 2021, when the economy was roaring back to life after cratering in the COVID-19 pandemic. With corporate profits up so much, while stock prices are still roughly where they were two months ago, stocks don’t look as expensive as they did before, according to Phil Segner, a co-portfolio manager at the Leuthold Group. Also helping stocks on Tuesday was another drop for oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, sank 5.4 per cent to $US79.25 per barrel as hope once again took over from fear in the oil market. It had swung sharply between $US72 and $US102 through July on uncertainty about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude around the world.



It’s jerked up and down many times as uncertainty built, receded and then built again, not only week to week but also hour to hour. Analysts warned more swings could still be ahead, but the latest drop in oil prices nevertheless helped to ease Wall Street’s worries about inflation. That in turn pulled down yields in the bond market, which relaxes pressure on the overall economy and on prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.63 per cent from 4.70 per cent Monday and from 4.75 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Higher yields make it more expensive for all kinds of Americans to borrow money, from homebuyers looking for a mortgage to big companies looking to build AI data centres. Related Article Opinion

Appliances He lied about an affair and cost his company nearly $30 million. Now he has a new job Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Reports on the US economy, meanwhile, showed it remains resilient even though inflation remains worse than anyone would like. One said US employers were advertising nearly 7.4 million job openings at the end of June, a slight slowdown from May’s level but close to economists’ expectations.



In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi had a more significant move and rose 1.6 per cent. Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings recently because its stock market is dominated by two companies swept up in AI mania, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The Kospi had dropped 5.1 per cent and soared 17.9 per cent in the prior two days. Stocks of computer chip companies also strengthened on Wall Street, where gains of 2.5 per cent for Nvidia, 6.6 per cent for Broadcom and 7.6 per cent for Micron Technology were some of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500.
