World.title: ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack David Crowe August 5, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A man selling vegetables in a Ukrainian town survived an attack by a Russian drone after it chased him around his vehicle in a chilling strike captured on video and shared around the world. The attack drew condemnation as an example of a “human safari” by Russian drone operators who watch for civilians and follow them with their airborne explosives in the manner of a computer game. Loading Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the attack as a crime and said the man under attack in the southern city of Kherson had been wounded in the blast. “A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him,” he said.



“Every single day, ordinary people in Kherson face these Russian ‘safaris’.” Kherson, located across the Dnipro River from Russian forces, has seen hundreds of drone attacks on civilians over the past year, leading local authorities to install netting and other barriers to try to protect citizens. Many of the city’s most important functions have been moved underground to escape the attacks, which became so commonplace that Ukrainians coined the term “human safari” for the Russian tactics. Warning: Graphic content View post on X



The drones are fitted with cameras to allow a “first-person view” by the Russian operator, who can look for a target, even if it is a civilian on a city street. The horrific video highlighted the scale of this threat by showing how the vegetable seller tried to hide from the drone as it hovered around his van. The man was identified as Yurii, 52, who came to Kherson from a nearby area to sell fresh produce, according to the Kyiv Independent and other Ukrainian media. The video shows him trying to dodge the drone, which hovers around and over the van, before the device detonates near him. He was taken to hospital suffering from shrapnel wounds and concussion. In a video released by the local military officials, Yurii said he was trying to show the drone operator that he was only selling vegetables. “But it started flying right at me,” he added. He said his wife was able to escape.



Drone operator is a ‘sadist’ Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the attack a “barbaric” Russian war crime and said thousands of similar attacks never reached the public eye. “This is a deliberate and systemic Russian strategy. They know exactly what they are doing. The sadist operating this drone knows full well that he is targeting a civilian,” he said. Drones have increased in speed and range to the point where the danger zone for soldiers and civilians can extend for 25 kilometres on either side of the front line, according to Ukrainian military officials. This “kill zone” is wide enough to include entire cities such as Kherson. When The New York Times reported on the “safaris” in January, local officials said about 200 civilians had been killed and 2000 wounded in the drone strikes over the past year.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war How dodging drones and death became daily life in eastern Ukraine In May, Ukrainian soldiers in Kherson told a reporter from London’s The Telegraph of the way they hacked into the feeds of the FPV drones to see the vision being relayed to a Russian operator, helping them identify the threats and destroy them. “On a busy day, we might shoot down ten drones,” the operator of the drone detection equipment told the newspaper. One Ukrainian aid worker recently told this masthead of a narrow escape from an FPV drone near a village outside Kharkiv, another city close to Russian forces. “There was an FPV drone just flying after our car, and I was terrified,” said Anastasiia Bilchenko. “We could see, from our drone detector, that the eyes of the drone were following us.”



The Kherson attack came one day after the widespread circulation of a video showing a Ukrainian drone falling on a Russian beach at a Black Sea resort crowded with civilians. Russian officials said seven people died, including three children, and another 58 were injured. Loading The video showed the drone falling at Gelendzhik, east of Crimea, and exploding on the beach. Russian authorities accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, while Ukrainian official Andriy Kovalenko said the drone had been shot down by Russian air defence personnel. Lastrina spotlights two big considerations when it comes to these arrangements. “The first is choosing the right person to live with. It goes beyond someone you get along with. They need to be someone that you consider financially disciplined. Someone you’ll be able to resolve conflict with, swiftly.” The second? “I absolutely believe all friends buying property together should have legal documents drawn up.” A “co-ownership agreement” can outline: How much each person initially contributed to the property

How mortgage repayments and bills are paid

How renovations, repayment defaults and disputes are treated

What happens if one owner wants to sell

And what happens if one owner loses decision-making capacity or dies Buyers should also investigate whether they need estate planning and/or family law advice, and to do so at the outset, before the property purchase. One of the biggest mistakes people make is failing to consider worst-case scenarios.



Lastrina recalls one case where two friends bought a property and one sadly passed away. The deceased’s share of the property was passed on to their younger sibling, as per their will. Editor's pick Opinion

Property investment Why Australians can no longer count on property to make them rich “The surviving owner now owns a property with a friend’s younger sibling, a person they don’t really know or trust. Because there was no co-ownership agreement in place, there was no mechanism that meant the surviving owner could easily purchase half of the property.” These agreements aren’t solely about mitigating scenarios as serious. There can be fun clauses, too. “One of my favourite clauses is that every six weeks, the parties have a meeting – almost like an AGM.” Karli and Mark were both single when they bought, which raises the million-dollar question: what happens if one of them enters a relationship?



“Ideally, the plan would be to rent the property out rather than add a third person into the considerations.” They’ve decided to discuss this further if the time comes and re-engage a lawyer. Lastrina says that people can stipulate what happens if an owner finds a partner in a co-ownership agreement. If this does happen, she recommends the couple sets up a binding financial agreement (Australia’s version of a prenup) giving them more certainty around how their respective interests would be dealt with if they separated, which can indirectly benefit co-owners by providing greater clarity in the event of relationship breakdowns. *These names have been changed. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.

World.title: Think soup is boring? These bowls bring colour, crunch and main meal energy
World.content:
From halloumi fries to crispy-skinned chicken, these hearty soups have the satisfying texture already built in. No side of bread required.

I love soup. But I know sceptics exist. To them, soup isn’t a meal unless it’s accompanied by a cheese-oozing toastie or a slab of sourdough the size of a world atlas.

Honestly? I respect that kind of aggressive dedication to dinner. But to save you the side-dish admin, I’ve skipped straight to the chase. Here are soups with the something-something already built in. We’re talking halloumi fries, dunkable spring rolls and hunks of gloriously crispy-skinned chicken. No sides required.

Halloumi “fries” launch zaatar-roasted tomato soup into a new flavour realm. Katrina Meynink

Zaatar-roasted tomato soup with halloumi fries

In culinary school, a German chef once admonished my “thick soup”, going on a tirade about Australians and our horrifying love for a dense puree. Consider me a proud, card-carrying thick-soup advocate until the end of my days. How else could a bowl carry the piping hot, salty squeak of tanned halloumi fries? It takes a standard tomato soup and pushes it into an entirely new realm of mealtime.

World.title: Five hurt, person arrested as witnesses say SUV hit cyclists in Epsom, dog killed
World.content:
A person has been arrested after reports a stolen car hit a group of cyclists, with five people hurt.

A dog was also killed at the scene during the incident in the Auckland suburb of Epsom, RNZ understands.

It's understood a man allegedly stole a car before he crashed into a group of cyclists.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Emergency services were called to the scene on Manukau Road around 7.05 on Wednesday morning.

Five patients were at the scene when Hato Hone St John arrived, a spokesperson confirmed.

A witness said he saw a man drive into a group of cyclists in what appeared to be a stolen car. Marika Khabazi / RNZ

Three were taken to hospital, one in critical condition, another with serious injuries and a third in a moderate condition.

Two other people were treated at the scene.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Several smashed vehicles could be seen inside the cordon, along with a crumpled bicycle next to a red puffer jacket.

Petrol station worker Manthan Patel said he heard a "crazy" sound before he witnessed a man driving a car crash into another vehicle.

He said the man then got out of the car and attacked a dog.

Emergency services were called to Manukau Road around 7.05 on Wednesday morning. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

A staff member at Forbes Homemade Gourmet on Ranfurly Rd told RNZ she had seen the incident unfold early this morning.

"There was a guy shouting in the streets next to where I'm working.

"It seemed as though he had no pants on."

She was worried that he could come into her workplace, so decided to call the police.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Soon after, customers told cafe staff that the man had crashed a car and punched a woman, she said.

A cordon put in place around the area had caused "bumper to bumper traffic" in the area, but it was now clearing, she said.

Another witness told the NZ Herald they saw the man fighting with a woman at the intersection of Manukau Rd and Mt St John Ave, where he "threw punches", knocking the woman to the ground and stealing her keys.

After taking off in an old SUV and damaging nearby vehicles, the witness told the Herald the man drove into a group of cyclists "hitting one and sending them flying over the top of the car".

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

A worker at Steam wand cafe just outside the Manukau Rd cordon said heard the man screaming about 7am, followed by the screams of a woman. Police sped past the cafe soon after.

Police have released limited information however, a cordon is in place on Manukau Rd between Ranfurly Rd and Queen Mary Ave.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Campbell Cres is closed to Puriri Dr.

Drivers have contacted RNZ reporting a backlog of traffic in the area.

In an alert to passengers, Auckland Transport said buses are not stopping in the area at present..

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

In a post on Twitter/X, MP for Epsom David Seymour said his thoughts were with those affected by the "horrible incident in our community".

"I will leave for police to communicate details of the incident, but there is no further danger since the one offender is in custody."

There will be an increased police presence in the area while enquiries are ongoing.

A cordon is in place on Manukau Rd between Ranfurly Rd and Queen Mary Ave. Marika Khabazi / RNZ

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

World.title: Transpower issues power warning
World.content:
Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Transpower says Wednesday morning's peak saw the highest-ever electricity use and it has issued a warning that there might be an energy shortfall on Friday morning.

It has put out a customer advice notice, which says a national energy shortfall or low residual generation had been identified on Friday from 7.30am until 8.30am.

Customer advice notices are aimed at power companies, rather than the general public.

Its executive general manager Chantelle Bramley said they were "actively managing the tight balance between supply and demand during this cold snap".

During this morning's peak, it saw the highest-ever electricity use at 7247 MW, she said.

Late Tuesday night a generation unit had a fault and was removed from service, she said.

"The power system remained secure and there was no impact on consumers."

Transpower was working closely with the industry to ensure that there was enough generation offered to cover the record demand, she said.

"At this stage we do not anticipate any impact on electricity supply to consumers."

Transpower had earlier issued warnings about Wednesday morning between 7.30 and 8.30, Wednesday evening between 6pm and 7pm and Thursday morning between 7.30 and 8.30.

It is requesting that power companies ensure energy, wind generation, reserve offers and load bids are accurate, increase their energy and reserve offers and increase transmission offers where generation could be constrained.

This is the first stage in the process of Transpower highlighting an issue. It can also issue warning notices from 36 hours out to one hour before a shortfall is expected, and grid emergency notices within one hour of an expected issue.

Powerswitch general manager Paul Fuge said the notices were issued when Transpower noticed high demand, to tell generators to submit their offers ahead of time so supply and demand could be managed. "It's their way of signalling to the market… so they know what's going on and they need them to submit bids."

He said it signalled that supply was tight and Transpower was trying to take prudent action to ensure it could meet demand.

A spokesperson for Meridian said the notices were not uncommon over winter. "We don't have any concerns and nor should the public. We're generating hard."

World.title: Only 57 percent of Kiwi children reach age 5 without tooth decay
World.content:
Parents are far too optimistic about how well their kids are looking after their teeth, and it is having serious consequences, a new report has found.

The New Zealand Dental Association report found 90 percent of parents said their children had "good" to "excellent" oral health, but only 57 percent of children reached age five without tooth decay.

Only 63 percent brushed twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.

The stats are part of the association's 2026 Oral Health Report Card which looks at every aspect of dental health - from family bathrooms to operating theatres

The data suggested parents might have a "false sense of security" about their children's health.

"...this high level of parental confidence may not accurately reflect underlying oral health status," the report said.

The association's president, and working dentist, Dave Excell said parents might be surprised about how much they need to be involved.

"I think sometimes parents think they can just leave their kids to do it themselves but they really need to be supervised up to the age of eight or nine, using a fluoride toothpaste, making sure they are doing a good job," he said.

But solving the problem was not just on parents.

Other statistics showed there were failings across the system - one example was that not enough children and teens were accessing free checkups they are entitled to every year.

There were likely several reason why - including wait lists, which were a post code lottery.

Children and teens in Hawkes Bay and Tairawhiti waited longer for dental appointments than anywhere else.

It was important to solve the problem which could have lifelong consequences, Excell said.

"You have to ask the question why at five years old, 43 percent of our children have got a completely preventable disease already," he said.

At the most serious end of the scale, about 4500 children were on the waiting list for hospital level dental care.

That number had got smaller by about 1000 over the past year but it was still too high, Excell said.

"Somewhere in the region of 7500 to 8000 children every year need a general anaesthetic to have their teeth sorted out and again that is just not acceptable in a country like ours," he said

Today's report aimed to bring together a number of measures, to get a snap shot of the country's oral health.

World.title: Live weather: Another icy morning, as temperatures plunge further
World.content:
Update from Metservice’s John Law as cold weather hits NZ Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Follow our liveblog above for the latest.

MetService says it's been one of the coldest mornings of the year and it's set to continue for the next two days.

Mt Cook at minus 8 or 9 degrees Celsius and Tekapo at minus 7 had the coldest starts to the day in the country.

Temperatures as far north as Auckland and Northland would be even colder overnight tonight, possibly producing frosts, meteorologist John Law says.

Taumauranui would possibly be at -6degC and Hamilton at -4degC on Thursday.

"So cold, frosty and really chilly."

Some highways are shut on Wednesday, including State Highway 1 between Waiouru and Rangipo (the Desert Road) and the Remutaka Hill Road near Wellington.

Transpower has issued a warning that there might be an energy shortfall this week.

It has put out a customer advice notice, which says a national energy shortfall or low residual generation had been identified on Friday from 7.30am until 8.30am.

It had earlier issued warnings this morning between 7.30 and 8.30, this evening between 6pm and 7pm and Thursday morning between 7.30 and 8.30.

It is requesting that power companies ensure energy, wind generation, reserve offers and load bids are accurate, increase their energy and reserve offers and increase transmission offers where generation could be constrained.

Meanwhile, an advocate for older people says many senior citizens are having to spend most of the day in bed because they can't afford to heat their homes.

World.title: Older Kiwis choosing between 'starving or heating' as price increases bite
World.content:
Age Concern’s Greta Bond discusses energy affordability Morning Report Download MP3 5m

An advocate for older people says recent cold temperatures combined with the cost of power and other goods have produced a crisis point, with many people forced to choose between food and heating.

Age Concern Canterbury chief executive Greta Bond told Morning Report older people on fixed incomes were having to make real choices every day about whether they will be warm or fed.

"Every week we're encountering people who are really struggling. Renters are in a particularly precarious position because they may be spending 60 or 70 percent of their pension on rent.

"It's actually a real crisis for people. I don't think people really understand or like to think that we have older people who are actively living in poverty in our country," Bond said.

Many people were resorting to spending most of their day in bed with negative consequences.

"They might get up for a little bit in the middle of the day when it's the most warm, probably not at all this week. They might just wake up in the morning, get themselves a cup of tea or something, and then just stay in bed the whole day.

"That's so bad for them in terms of their health, their physical health, their mental health, their social connection, but definitely staying in a really constricted life because they can't go out. And they might not even leave their bedroom."

While the increased costs hit those renting hard, Bond said retired home owners were also vulnerable to price rises for different reasons.

"While you have the security of tenure, you're your own landlord, so you may not have a healthy home in terms of the insulation, and maintenance may be difficult. So that home may be even colder than the rental," she said.

"As a society, we need to think about our older people and what we are prioritising.

"We aren't a country, I think, who would like to think of the fact that we've got old people who are either starving or freezing in their own homes. And, at a government level, I'd like to see more attention to that. But also individually, we can look out for our older neighbours as well," she said.

The Winter Energy Payment was welcome but it was not enough.

World.title: Veteran radio broadcaster hangs up the mic, aged 93
World.content:
A 93-year-old veteran of community radio broadcasting is hanging up his microphone after 25 years on air.

Ray Woodley has presented an assortment of music programmes in Palmerston North and he has just recorded the 700th - and last - episode of his latest show Musical Confection.

A builder by trade, Woodley only began broadcasting after he retired, but he says he has loved every minute of it.

RNZ sat in with Woodley for some of his final recording, which began: "Greetings everybody for this programme, Musical Confection, programme number 700 - how did I ever get to here?

"They've given me an hour today, so I'm going to play lots of tracks I have liked over the years - whether anybody else did, I don't know."

Ray Woodley has broadcast on community radio in Palmerston North for 25 years. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Woodley has presented Musical Confection since 2011. It mainly focused on big band classics and jazz standards.

There were many other programmes in the decade before that too on the airwaves of Manawatū People's Radio - one of 12 community stations throughout New Zealand - as well as stints as an announcer and even board chairman.

"I can still remember driving my car up Rangitīkei Street for the first time, nervous as billy-o, and never thinking I'd get to 700 programmes, of this one," he said of his radio debut.

Woodley showed some emotion as he unpacked CDs neatly stacked in his briefcase and cast a last final eye over his programme's runlist.

"I've got mixed feelings about today, but that's what happens in life - parts of your life come to an end."

The end of an era did not go unmarked - a portrait of Woodley was unveiled on the radio station wall. It was drawn by radio station content co-ordinator Hugh Dingwall's daughter Leilani.

A likeness of Ray Woodley now hangs on the Manawatū People's Radio wall. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

And as Woodley took a break from recording his extended farewell, there was time for a few stories over a glass of alcohol-free bubbles, including the time he was on air and a woman phoned in with a request.

She wanted to hear a song she insisted was well known, Share Your Banana With Me.

Woodley said he was stumped, so consulted the then-station manager, who eventually worked out the caller meant Kiwi classic, Sir John Rowles' Cheryl Moana Marie, which Woodley played on air. The woman rang back, thankful to learn the song's real name.

Woodley said the nerves of his early days were gone, although he admitted he was not as confident as he once was.

But he was grateful the small team at Manawatū People's Radio looked after him.

Dingwall said Woodley was full of surprises, and was a generous man who would regularly bring in fresh produce from his garden.

"He's definitely going to be missed," Dingwall said.

"Because he lives at Olive Tree, at a rest home, he's in direct contact with a lot of people who are his listeners, in a way that's quite unusual for our shows.

"He'll get people knocking on his door saying, That was a good one you did, Ray."

Ray Woodley was at time emotional as he began his final recording, aged 93. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Woodley was a stalwart of the Manawatū music scene, Dingwall said.

"In many ways he's kind of a last window into a world of music that doesn't exist any more. He had an early career as an itinerant piano player.

"There was a period of time where every building had a piano, so if you were having a party you hired a guy to come and play it, and in Manawatū that guy was Ray. He had to know every popular song off the top of his head."

Woodley is also a banjo player and, around his day job, managed bands.

He will now have a gap in his weekly schedule, which he said he would probably fill with more lunches and more piano playing at the rest home.

"It does seem a bit strange. I'll probably find for a couple of weeks I might think, hello, what should I be doing today?

"It's my 25th year and 700 programmes - it's probably a good time to call it off."

World.title: BNZ increases home loan rates
World.content:
Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

BNZ has become the latest bank to put up its home loan rates.

It is increasing its standard one-year rate by 20 basis points to 4.99 percent.

The 18-month rate also increases by the same margin, to 5.29 percent.

Two- and three-year rates will lift by 16 basis points and four-year rates by six, all to 5.45 percent.

It follows ANZ, which said increases were due to rising wholesale rates.

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said financial markets had priced in the official cash rate getting to 3 percent or slightly above by the end of this year and 3.5 percent by the middle of next year.

"That's in line with our forecast, pretty much all of what I expected is already priced into rates. You might get another 10 basis points, maybe slightly more on the one-year rate before the end of the year but I don't see a great deal of pressure on the one-year rates past that.

"Even through 2027 as the expected rate increases become reality you might get a bit more but I'm talking about a one-year rate at maybe 5.4 percent and the two-year at 5.7 percent. It's not huge, assuming the world behaves itself, there's not massive amounts of lift left."

He said it was unlikely that home loan rates would get into the 6 percent range again.

World.title: Should customers pay less when they use a self-checkout?
World.content:
Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Who is really saving money when supermarket shoppers check out and bag their own groceries?

That is a question New York lawmakers have reportedly been pondering.

State representative Nikki Lucas has introduced a bill that would require retail businesses selling food in the state to offer a 10 percent discount to those who used the self-checkout lane.

"Retail businesses increasingly rely on self-checkout systems to reduce staffing and operational costs by shifting responsibilities traditionally performed by employees onto consumers," she wrote.

Who really benefits from self checkout machines? Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"Since customers are effectively completing portions of the checkout labor themselves without compensation, providing a mandatory discount helps ensure fairness, acknowledges consumer participation in store operations, and allows the public to share in the financial savings created by self-service technology."

Consumer NZ head of advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said her organisation thought there was validity to the argument in New Zealand, too.

"If you're serving yourself then ultimately the supermarket is saving money through less staff resourcing, and those savings are not currently being passed on to shoppers.

"Pak'n Save advertises themselves as a cheaper place to shop given you pack your bags yourself. It seems many businesses are moving towards fewer staff and more technological assistance, for example there are now fewer bank branches across New Zealand, and more chatbots instead of call centre representatives across a number of major businesses. Ultimately this provides a cost saving for the business, not the consumer."

She said concern about the price of food and groceries was still the number one financial worry for most people.

"When we started tracking financial concerns in 2022, food pricing was the 8th highest concern. Lowering prices for shoppers who choose to self-serve would be one way to alleviate some of these cost pressures, however we're dubious the supermarkets would introduce such a discount."

University of Auckland marketing expert Professor Michael Lee said it made sense from a fairness point-of-view.

"The supermarkets are saving ongoing cost of labour by automating that portion of their operations. Therefore, why not to pass on the savings to their loyal customers?"

He said in a market like New Zealand, it was unlikely that retailers would make the choice to offer a discount, unless they were compelled to.

"Unless one of the retailers, or a new entrant, decided to take this approach, there would little incentive for either to do so, meaning that the two main retailers would continue to use such cost savings to extend their profit margin."

Foodstuffs said self-checkouts were one of a number of ways customers could choose to shop, alongside traditional staffed checkouts.

"Many customers value the convenience, speed and flexibility that self-service offers, particularly when buying a small number of items. We continue to invest in both self-service and staffed checkouts so customers can choose the option that best suits their needs. Team members are always available to assist customers using self-checkouts and to operate staffed lanes. Our focus is on giving customers choice and making shopping as easy and convenient as possible."

Woolworths said in a statement it thought customers found it convenient to have options.

World.title: Embattled FIFA boss faces 'blackmail' allegations from ex-staffer
World.content:
Former FIFA vice president Prince Ali bin Al Hussein has criticised the football body's leadership headed by Gianni Infantino, describing prize money withheld from his Jordan national team as a kind of blackmail.

Prince Ali said the Jordanian federation he leads still has not been paid money due for reaching the final of the FIFA Arab Cup played last December in Qatar.

In a social media post, Prince Ali said that during the World Cup — where Jordan made its debut in June — he was told if he endorsed FIFA president Gianni Infantino "it would go a long way to helping our FA out".

Mr Infantino is under pressure to save his 11-year presidency amid a fierce backlash from global football leaders about his now-failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

"We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now," said Prince Ali, who placed third in a five-candidate FIFA presidential contest when Infantino was first elected in February 2016.

"But the whole situation amounts to blackmail, and we refuse to give in to that," the Jordanian royal wrote.

FIFA Arab Cup money not paid

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (left) was on hand to present Morocco the trophy after the Arab Cup final against Jordan last year. (Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The 2025 FIFA Arab Cup that Jordan lost in the title match against Morocco was set to pay $4.2 million to the beaten finalist, Jordanian media reported last year.

"The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet," Prince Ali wrote, "while at the same time FIFA brags about how many billions they have in reserve."

"It is clear the problem really is with leadership. For months, FIFA has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters," he said.

FIFA was approached for comment about the claims.

Prince Ali's FIFA history

Prince Ali Bin Al Hussein (right) and Gianni Infantino (left) look on during a FIFA Congress meeting in 2016. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

Prince Ali was elected by Asian football to serve on FIFA's ruling executive committee from 2011-15, and stood against then-president Sepp Blatter in a May 2015 election. That vote to re-elect Blatter was held in the shadow of raids at Zurich hotels two days earlier to arrest football officials as part of investigations by US and Swiss federal agencies.

Mr Infantino had seemed a lock to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term leading FIFA through 2031 when he left New York two weeks after the World Cup final.

Fallout from his secretive private equity plan revealed one week ago has rocked soccer politics, with Mr Infantino's former colleagues at European football body UEFA now looking for a rival candidate.

The proposal underwritten by Mr Kushner's Thrive Eternal fund would have paid $20 million each to Jordan and all other FIFA members had they accepted by a September 19 deadline

UEFA is also threatening a boycott of FIFA games, events and meetings, while the leadership of the North American soccer body CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation, of which Jordan is a member, have also spoken out against Mr Infantino.

FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for candidates to declare for the election by 211 member federations on March 18 in Rabat, Morocco.

AP

World.title: NRLW great Ali Brigginshaw gets three-match ban
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos skipper Ali Brigginshaw has been handed a three-week ban for a dangerous tackle and will miss a major chunk of the rest of the NRLW home-and-away season.

Brigginshaw was sent straight to the judiciary for her tackle on Canterbury's Tayla Preston during Magic Round at Wagga Wagga.

The Broncos lead the competition with a 5-0 record, but Brigginshaw will now be unavailable until round 9, three games before the finals series.

As Preston ran the ball away from her goal line, Brigginshaw advanced and grabbed the Bulldogs player, then spun her around before lifting her up and bringing her down on her head.

Preston avoided serious injury and Brigginshaw was charged with a grade 3 dangerous throw.

Brigginshaw thanked the judiciary panel for considering her case and reiterated her remorse for the incident.

"I meant absolutely no malice in making the tackle, I apologised to Tayla post-match and have been in contact with her again since, she was accepting of my apology on both occasions," she said.

"I'm looking forward to getting back on the field in a few weeks and finishing my playing career on a positive note."

The 36-year-old, who is playing her final season of NRLW before retirement, has not missed a Broncos game since the competition's inception in 2018.

Sydney Roosters forward Aliyah Nasio was the last NRLW player to be referred directly to the judiciary following a brawl at the conclusion of last year's grand final, when she struck Brisbane's Julia Robinson.

Nasio was banned for four matches after being hit with a grade 3 striking charge.

In 2023, Parramatta's Kennedy Cherrington was also banned for four weeks after being charged with a grade 3 dangerous throw.

World.title: Clarkson happy with handshake to extend contract as North set to miss finals
World.content:
North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson is unfazed going into the final year of his contract, saying he just needs a "handshake".

As Clarkson comes towards the end of his fourth season in charge, North will spend a 10th-straight year without experiencing finals action.

Speculation has started to mount that Kangaroos hierarchy might consider letting Clarkson go at the end of his current five-year deal, signed in late 2022 in what was a massive coup for the club.

Although North have improved this year, they are yet to beat a team above them on the ladder and will fall short of a wildcard berth.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

"Old school" Clarkson will not be pushing for a contract extension beyond 2027 this off-season and is happy to wait it out.

"All I require is a handshake and a wink and a nod, and that'll do me," the four-time Hawthorn premiership coach said on Tuesday.

"We'll work our way through whatever we need to do.

"I'm really here to serve the footy club … it's not just me, but those that are in leadership positions at the club have done a really good job stabilising the footy club.

"We're really keen to progress and get ourselves up the ladder, but all we do know is that that's done best when you've got stability."

Clarkson drew on examples of Brisbane Lions, Fremantle and Adelaide of clubs who were patient with their coaches and find themselves in powerful positions on the field.

"I've been in the caper for a long time, so that's a bit of water off the duck's (back)," he said of speculation about his future.

"The best examples are the reigning premiers (Brisbane) who took a while to get going and then Adelaide with 'Nicksy' (Matthew Nicks) and Fremantle with Justin Longmuir.

"The governance and administration of the club just sticking to the path and sticking to the course, and we're going to be no different."

Clarkson's record at North is 19-1-59, a far cry from his glory years with the Hawks.

The Kangaroos face a challenging run home, starting with the Western Bulldogs at Docklands on Thursday night.

They have long losing streaks against the Bulldogs, and their final two opponents, Geelong and Sydney.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Clarkson bristled when asked how important it would be to beat one of those teams to finish off this season.

"You're just searching, searching for a headline," he said.

"Teams that have been in the bottom four or five on the ladder haven't beaten the top teams very often in the last five or six years.

"That's the reason why they've been in that position on the ladder."

AAP

World.title: Clubs stand firm after AFL's controversial finals memo
World.content:
The AFL's warning to clubs about resting players before the newly introduced wildcard round has not gone down well with coaches.

Clubs have been threatened with sanctions if they decide to make mass changes for their games in round 24.

"While legitimate player management of player fatigue or injuries is permitted, the AFL will scrutinise club team selection decisions in the lead-up to AFL finals," AFL football boss Greg Swann wrote in a memo to clubs on Monday.

The AFL has had a pre-finals bye since 2016, allowing the top-eight teams a week off before the last month of the season.

But with the finals system effectively becoming a top-10 due to the wildcard weekend, not every club will be afforded that luxury should they qualify.

Teams ranked seventh to 10th at the end of the home-and-away season will have to back up and play the following week.

The top-six will all rest before preparing for respective qualifying and elimination finals, starting on September 3.

The Western Bulldogs are almost certain to finish in the wildcard bracket, creating a dilemma for coach Luke Beveridge.

"The main consideration for the teams who might be certainties to play a wildcard game going into that round is the fact that the six teams above the seventh have all got a week off," Beveridge told Fox Footy.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I'm sure within the ranks of the teams that are certainties, you're processing who needs a week off.

"I'd question how the AFL could question a club, because you're questioning the medical department from a club as well, if that happens."

Steven King, in his rookie season as Melbourne coach, was also left perplexed by the AFL's directive.

"I'm the coach of the Melbourne footy club," he told Fox Footy.

"I'll make any decision that's best for our football club and best for the management of our players."

The Dockers made a string of changes for the last home-and-away round in 2013, then travelled to Geelong and beat the Cats in finals. (Getty Images: Michael Dodge)

Fremantle famously made 10 changes for their final home-and-away game in 2013, leading to them being thrashed by struggling St Kilda.

The following week, the Dockers pulled off a historic qualifying-final win in Geelong over the highly fancied Cats.

In 2015, North Melbourne rested nine players ahead of a finals campaign when they lost against Richmond.

The move paid off for the Kangaroos, who turned the tables on the Tigers in an elimination final and also won a semi-final in Sydney.

Former North Melbourne coach Brad Scott rested nine players in the final round of the 2015 season, while Ross Lyon made 10 changes in the final round of the 2013 season when he was in charge of Fremantle.

World.title: Aussie swimmer out of leadership group after reported drinking session
World.content:
Australian swimmer Isaac Cooper has stepped down from the Dolphins's leadership group after a drinking session at the Commonwealth Games.

Cooper was reported to be out drinking when he was expected to be supporting teammates at Glasgow's Tollcross International Swimming Centre last Wednesday night.

Cooper was also seen drinking at the Australian team hotel during that day, the report said.

"Isaac did not attend the final night of the swimming competition or final team meeting in Glasgow, which is in conflict with team expectations," a Swimming Australia statement said.

What the Commonwealth Games mean is up to you Australian chef de mission and eight-time Olympic medallist Petria Thomas cried as she spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth Games to her, so it doesn't really matter if it felt too easy for Australia at times.

"Isaac has since voluntarily stood down from the team's athlete leadership group."

Cooper was scheduled to race the 100m backstroke final that night but withdrew from the event after qualifying eighth-fastest.

Swimmers were expected to support teammates at the Glasgow Games when not racing, while Cooper also missed the team meeting that night.

The 22-year-old won gold at the Glasgow Games as a member of the 4x100m medley team after swimming in the heats.

He also finished sixth in the 50m backstroke final, an event he won a silver medal at the 2024 world championships.

Cooper will next compete at the Pan Pacific championships in the United States starting August 12.

World.title: Blues announce King as new Origin coach after Daley steps down
World.content:
Former NSW State of Origin player Matt King has been named the new head coach of the Blues.

King was announced as the new coach on Tuesday after predecessor Laurie Daley stepped down from the role on Monday.

Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach The NSWRL pays tribute to Blues "hero" Laurie Daley as the coach stands down from his role after this year's series win over Queensland.

King played nine times for the Blues from 2005-2007, and over 200 first grade matches for Melbourne, South Sydney and Warrington across the NRL and Super League in England.

"I'm very clear on what it looks like to be the head coach of NSW," King said.

"I have a true understanding of what it means to lead this great state of ours and I can't wait for that opportunity.

"The one true rugby league love of my life has been the NSW Blues. To know now that I have the opportunity to guide the team moving forward, to lead the program over the next little period, means the absolute world to me."

The 45-year-old has been a long-time assistant coach under Trent Robinson at the Sydney Roosters, and has been part of the Blues' coaching staff since 2024.

Daley stepped down as Blues coach on Monday after guiding NSW to a series win this year.

The Blues sealed the series with a 30-12 triumph in the decider at Lang Park, just the fourth time NSW has won a deciding Game III in Brisbane.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said in a statement on Monday.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

World.title: Haugset goes it alone to claim Tour de France Femmes third stage
World.content:
Sigrid Haugset has set off on a long solo run and kept going to the finish to win the third stage of the Women's Tour de France and claim the yellow jersey.

The Norwegian rider made her break with more than half of the tough 156.5-kilometre route between Geneva and Poligny to go.

The stage featured four categorised climbs and Haugset made her move with 85 kilometres left, at the foot of the category two Col de la Savine.

Haugset was also first across the last listed climb of the day, the category four Côte de Chaux-Champagny, followed by Lotte Kopecky about 30 seconds behind, and a nine-rider group more than two minutes adrift.

Previous yellow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes, who won the first two stages, was 13 minutes behind with the main bunch at the time. She ultimately finished more than 20 minutes adrift of Haugset and dropped to 67th in the general classification.

It was a battle between two riders going into the last 10 kilometres. Kopecky had cut Haugset's lead to 15 seconds and the Belgian rider could just about see her rival ahead.

But Haugset, sensing the danger, stood on her pedals to stay ahead and managed to increase her lead again, finishing 1:24 ahead of Kopecky.

Haugset leads the general classification by 2:02 from Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius, with 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering third, a further four seconds behind.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women's Tour, covers 1,175 kilometres over nine days.

World.title: Infantino could face UEFA lawsuit as he scrambles for FIFA presidency support
World.content:
European football body UEFA has threatened FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors, and says potential evidence should not be destroyed.

Mr Infantino on Saturday dropped a secretive proposal to raise $US4.2 billion ($6 billion) from investors, including the New York investment firm of Joshua Kushner, days after media reports revealed it, provoking a global furore.

UEFA led the backlash and its 55 member federations met to agree to boycott all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active.

Now UEFA's lawyers have informed FIFA that the European body is "actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints … arising out of and in connection with the FFE (FIFA Forward Enterprise) plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters".

The letter named 18 FIFA executives who it said should retain data, documents and electronic messages as potential evidence. They include Mr Infantino, Zurich-based chief finance officer Thomas Peyer and Arsène Wenger, the coaching great who is FIFA's head of global football development.

Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke Two of football's major bodies launch stinging rebukes of FIFA boss Gianni Infantino after his failed privatisation ploy.

"UEFA puts you on formal notice that any destruction, deletion, alteration, concealment, or loss of relevant materials following receipt of this notice — or following any earlier date on which you were, or reasonably should have been, aware that proceedings were anticipated — may constitute spoliation of evidence," the letter said.

Meanwhile, the Swedish football federation confirmed that UEFA is actively looking "to come up with an alternative candidate" as FIFA president. The next election is scheduled in March.

On Saturday, UEFA signalled it wants to end Mr Infantino's decade-long presidency, saying he had lost the confidence of world football and that "no option should be off the table".

Hours earlier, Mr Infantino had withdrawn the divisive proposal that offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each with a mid-September deadline to accept.

The FFE spin-off valued by FIFA at $20 billion would have taken control of the football body's money-making commercial and tournament operations through at least 2038. It promised to more than double development money over that time for the 211 members who already effectively own the Zurich-based not-for-profit governing body.

It was the project of just one man, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a stinging statement that said staff felt deceived by their boss Mr Infantino.

FIFA COO Kevin Lamour has made clear his opposition to Gianni Infantino's plan. (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

Legal proceedings are "reasonably anticipated," UEFA's lawyer Andrew J Levander wrote, citing the belief of football stakeholders that the plan was "fundamentally incompatible with the proper governance of football".

UEFA has been outspoken against its former employee Mr Infantino, while the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF also made strong statements opposing Mr Infantino's plan.

Mr Infantino has most support from his traditional base in Africa, while South America's CONMEBOL is relying on him to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams from 48. That would give more hosting games to Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, the home country of CONMEBOL president Alejandro Dominguez.

Gianni Infantino is reportedly seeking support from Donald Trump in his FIFA presidency battle. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Mr Infantino's path to stabilising the presidency he has held for more than 10 years was unclear. A report yesterday claimed he was seeking support from the administration of his close ally US President Donald Trump, possibly in a call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"There are no plans for @SecRubio to speak with Mr Infantino and there is no call this morning," Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of state for global public affairs, posted on social media.

The 56-year-old FIFA leader left New York after the World Cup final two weeks ago seemingly a lock to be re-elected unopposed next March for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

FIFA briefed at the World Cup that Mr Infantino had pledged letters of support from about 200 of the 211 member federations.

Those letters are now likely being withdrawn across Europe, with the Wales federation the first to announce its reversal.

The candidate deadline is November 18 for an election four months later in Morocco.

Tech.title: Now you can securely link multiple phones to one Signal account
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

You can link more devices with one phone number on Signal now, including an Android phone or iPhone. Signal already supported linking PCs and iPads, but not additional phones. When you link a device on Signal, you can check and respond to new messages across all of your linked devices. You can also choose whether or not to transfer an end-to-end encrypted copy of your previous messages to each newly linked device to mitigate the risk of devices that might be shared, lost, or compromised.

The update is rolling out now with Signal version 8.20 on Android and version 8.22 for iPhone / iPad.

Signal also says it has made “significant interface improvements to better support large devices,” including several improvements for foldable phones, which helped enable support for Android tablets. However, Signal says the large-screen version of its Android app is “still a work in progress,” and that it’s working on optimizing the interface for its Chromebook app, as well.

Tech.title: AMD’s datacenter business is booming while gaming takes a backseat
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Driven by demand for AI capacity, AMD’s data center revenue more than doubled year-over-year in its latest earnings report, reaching $6.7 billion. That’s up from $5.8 billion in Q1, and jumping 107 percent from the $3.2 billion it reported for the same period a year ago.

At the same time, AMD’s gaming revenue fell 31 percent compared to last year, to $779 million, as price hikes and component shortages slowed sales for the Xbox Series X / S, PS5, and Valve’s Steam Deck.

Image: AMD

“Revenue increased 50 percent year-over-year to a record $11.5 billion, driven by continued strength in our Data Center business, which represented 58% of company revenue in the quarter,” wrote AMD CFO Jean Hu. Its overall PC and gaming business revenue grew six percent compared to last year, with Client revenue up 23 percent thanks to Ryzen processor sales.

“AI is driving a significant expansion in demand for compute across all of our markets, and our leadership portfolio and growing customer visibility position us exceptionally well to capture this expanding opportunity and deliver substantial revenue and earnings growth in the years ahead,” said AMD CEO Lisa Su.

Tech.title: SpaceX made more revenue as an AI company than a space company
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

SpaceX’s AI revenue grew more than three times to $2.6 billion from the year before, mostly because of deals that the company made to provide compute to other AI companies, according to SpaceX’s quarterly earnings. The AI division, which the company said in its documents to go public was the source of most of its value, lost $1.5 billion this quarter, slightly less than in the same quarter last year.

SpaceX made deals with Anthropic in May and Google in June to provide compute to the other two AI companies, putting it in competition with other neoclouds such as CoreWeave. The increased presence in AI is also driving the company to spend more — capital expenditures reached $18.37 billion.

“We’re building AI compute capacity at scale faster than anyone else, we believe, and we’re significantly improving our AI models,” Elon Musk said on an investor call.

Despite its name, SpaceX said in the documents for its IPO that it expected most of its value to come from AI. SpaceX had the biggest-ever IPO in June. One of the things that the company said it could do better than anyone else was build data centers in space. The company has three segments: space, AI, and “connectivity,” which is the Starlink internet service. Space had $962 million in revenue this quarter, and SpaceX remained the biggest user of SpaceX rockets. The Starlink service had $4.2 billion in revenue.

Grok, SpaceX’s AI model that has been in hot water for undressing women and children without their consent, had fallen far behind other companies in the AI race. So before the IPO, SpaceX rented out the data center capacity it had initially built for itself. The company also agreed to acquire Cursor, providing it with an enterprise AI product. The acquisition has not yet closed, though Musk said on the call they’re “close to that,” but didn’t want to “jump the gun” on regulatory approval.

SpaceX is still losing money, but the loss this quarter narrowed to $143 million dollars. Musk’s grandiose plans — data centers in space, an addressable user market of more than the US GDP — don’t just come with a big price tag in AI. The costs of developing technology in its space division also rose by $389 million from the year before, with Starship as the primary driver of spending. Starship is key to Musk’s plan to expand its connectivity business, the only profitable part of the company.

Starship has to be able to launch heavier versions of the satellites that make its Starlink internet business profitable. Some of these satellites have already been manufactured, and in today’s documents, SpaceX said it had launched 20 of them. It’s not clear how far away the full deployment — of 60 satellites at once — is.

Though SpaceX beat analyst estimates, according to Bloomberg, its shares declined after market, following an initial pop of enthusiasm.

Update 5:40PM ET August 4th: Adds revenue from space and connectivity sectors of the business, as well as details on SpaceX’s history with AI, and details from the investor call.

Tech.title: EA is now a private company
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Electronic Arts has officially become a private company. Last September, EA announced that an investor group led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners would be taking the company private in a $55 billion deal, and on Tuesday, EA said the deal successfully closed. The PIF will reportedly own 93.4 percent of the new company.

The deal includes $20 billion of debt financing — making it the largest leveraged buyout ever — which could mean big changes at EA to justify the deal. As of late, EA has been focusing heavily on its big tentpole franchises, including things like Battlefield, its sports games like EA Sports FC and Madden NFL, and The Sims. Given the stakes of the deal, it seems likely that EA will depend more on bankable releases rather than experimenting on smaller games — a strategy that many of the industry’s biggest publishers, including Ubisoft and Xbox, are shifting toward as well.

”As we begin this next chapter, I’m more optimistic than ever about what we’ll create together,” CEO Andrew Wilson said in a message to staff. “The opportunities ahead are extraordinary, and they’ll be brought to life by our creativity, our ambition, and our belief in what’s possible.”

The deal for EA follows other major video game industry acquisitions in recent years, including Microsoft’s $68.7 billion deal for Activision Blizzard, its $7.5 billion deal for Bethesda Softworks parent company ZeniMax Media, and Take-Two’s $12.7 billion deal for Zynga.

Tech.title: Telegram CEO says an extortionist planted CSAM in a chat to get it pulled from the App Store
Tech.content:
Last night Apple briefly removed Telegram from the AppStore because a user had planted illegal porn in a public chat.

Telegram was restored within hours. But I want to explain what happened — to warn other app developers and help protect online communities from similar attacks.

Because Telegram quickly removes illegal content from public groups using all kinds of moderation tools, the attacker had to resort to a technical trick. He inserted AI-modified illegal content by editing an old message in an active group chat. As a result the content was effectively hidden from the group’s members, preventing them from seeing/reporting it.

The attacker was a takedown extortionist: someone who demands ransom from group owners in exchange for not targeting their communities. These extortionists use automated accounts to plant illegal content in public groups and then report it directly to Apple, attempting to trigger the removal of legitimate communities whose owners refused to pay them.

From a practical standpoint, illegal pornographic content in Telegram’s public groups is not a systemic problem. Our moderation is effective. The fact that attackers must resort to backdated, effectively invisible content and other technical tricks proves this.

⚠️ However, there are two important lessons here for app developers and online communities:

— Extortionists have found a way to manipulate Apple into overreacting. Apple removed Telegram from the App Store before contacting us. This creates a potential systemic risk for every mobile app that hosts user-generated content. If an app used by more than a billion people can be removed from the App Store without prior warning, any app can be.

— The tactics used by takedown extortionists are evolving, putting communities across social platforms at risk. Telegram has extensive experience identifying the tricks used by coordinated reporting gangs and protecting legitimate communities (even when doing so risks our own app being temporarily removed from the App Store). Other platforms may not be equally prepared.

Stay vigilant! ☝️

Tech.title: How an OpenAI influencer trip backfired
Tech.content:
The brand trip is a right of passage for influencers. It’s a mark of legitimacy that a sponsor wants to invite them on an all-expenses-paid vacation, often with luxurious freebies and activities. Trips can also spur hard feelings from uninvited influencers, trigger criticism from the public, and project a certain frivolousness.

Usually it is fast fashion companies or beauty brands flying out influencers with the goal of flooding social media with sponsored content. This time, it was a major AI company.

Over the weekend, several influencers began posting about OpenAI’s “first ever brand trip,” which appears to have taken place outside of New York City at a nature-filled retreat (for those curious, it looks to be the Instagram-bait Wildflower Farms). The trip was marketed as “Summer Club,” and influencers posted photos and videos from their cabins, showing off branded merch and monogrammed pajamas and talking vaguely about the scheduled programming. Many of the content creators appear to be in the career and business niches, posting about workplace culture or about being CEOs. Grace McCarrick, who has 145,000 followers on TikTok, vlogged from her suite as she ran a bath at night. Another influencer, Nat Lucy (57,000 followers), filmed herself spotting a deer outside of her cabin. All hell broke loose.

“People will literally sell their soul and their planet down the river for a nice free hotel room,” one commenter on TikTok wrote under McCarrick’s video. “Wow! Beautiful greenery! They should put a data center there!” reads a comment on Lucy’s post. Most of the videos got relatively little traction: McCarrick’s video has just under 300 likes, and Lucy’s video has fewer than 15,000 views. It’s measly engagement compared to what other splashy brand trips can command — but videos reacting to the trip have made it something of a scandal (a pair of clips alone has over half a million combined views).

Many of the comments on the influencers’ videos cite the environmental effects of the AI boom, the contentious buildout of data centers across the US, and the potential for job replacement or job loss as a result of companies integrating AI in the workplace. Some also questioned why so many of the content creators who went on the trip appeared to be young women, as if OpenAI was targeting a specific demographic via media they were more connected to (though based on photos and videos posted to social media, there were men on the trip, too). According to Pew, even as the AI usage gap between men and women has all but disappeared, women tend to view AI more negatively and are twice as likely to say AI will negatively impact them personally. Some audiences wondered whether female influencers were essentially being used to launder the reputation of an industry under scrutiny.

McCarrick, who describes herself as a creator who talks about “soft skills we need at work to millions online and to teams like Spotify, Amazon, Uber and DoorDash,” has since made multiple videos responding to commenters accusing her of essentially abandoning her morals for a fancy trip. On LinkedIn she wrote that she “genuinely had no idea that people were this anti-AI,” and that the negative response to her videos exposed her to “the shocking AI psychosis running rampant online” — by which she means anger about AI, not the more common definition of being driven to paranoia or delusions of grandeur by using AI. People in the real world “do not run around like a chicken with their heads cut off, screaming about water usage and wildlife and (curiously) fascism,” she wrote.

None of the influencers The Verge reached out to responded to requests for comment. OpenAI said creator marketing is part of how they reach people and that the event was meant to be educational.

“Creators are an important part of our community and how people get information and learn about our products today,” OpenAI spokesperson Edie Campbell-Urban said in an email. “We welcome healthy debate as AI becomes more prevalent, and we value creators who choose to engage with us, attend our events, ask tough questions, and learn alongside everyone else. We’ll continue to value them, just as we do traditional media and other marketing partners.”

Setting aside the backlash to the trip for a moment, a few things stand out. First, all things considered, this appears to be a relatively simple trip. That’s not to say it wasn’t luxurious — the rooms at the retreat cost upwards of $2,000 a night — but it is nothing compared to the brands that go all out in order to milk content from every last moment (some commenters poked fun at the fact that it was a domestic trip, not a far-flung, international vacation). Second, there’s a sense that everyone involved is testing the waters: Multiple influencers noted it was the first brand trip they’d attended, and one influencer indicated they were not paid for their attendance, which big brands often do for top talent. Third and most interestingly, the goals of the trip are muddled: It’s not entirely clear what the influencers were actually doing on the trip, because there is surprisingly little content online from the event. Typically, if an influencer is on a brand trip it’s inescapable — every little luxury, every meal, every activity is TikToked and photo dumped. Instead of content about the capabilities of ChatGPT, the videos and photos are largely aspirational lifestyle content focused on the free swag and pretty setting — and even then, there’s a conspicuous lack of content, period. There isn’t the same flood of picturesque montages, clips from expert sessions or Q&As, or summaries of what a creator learned from their time with OpenAI. At least not yet.

AI companies have used influencer marketing in straightforward ways, like paying creators to make content about their product offerings. But they’ve also dabbled in the kind of influencer marketing people expert from more traditional consumer brands: Anthropic has hosted more lowkey influencer dinners at trendy locations with lifestyle influencers, and there are rumblings of a second OpenAI trip on the West Coast.

As backlash to the industry has grown, AI companies have adjusted how they communicate with the public: “Your jobs will soon be obsolete” has clearly not been the right framing for why people should trust these companies or get on board with their mission. Instead, AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have tried to add a bit of human touch, whether that’s through in-person pop-up coffee shops, stylized merch drops, or ad campaigns that take concerns people have about AI and try to turn them into pro-AI inspirational content.

What better way to reach consumers directly than through the talking heads they already know and trust? Influencers are a convenient vessel, both for brands looking to disseminate their message and for the inevitable backlash from audiences who give them a platform in the first place. In this case, the content broke containment out of the girlboss-style business circles into the mainstream — an AI brand trip dressed up as an aspirational lifestyle retreat is both confusing and enraging to a public fatigued by this line of work. By tapping a certain kind of creator for a weekend of sponsored content, OpenAI is able to test a new audience without fully committing; it’s the content creators, after all, who will get the angry comments, whose faces will be plastered on the backgrounds of an ever-increasing number of reaction videos (influencers received similar backlash for a Shein brand trip in 2023). The AI industry wants the soft power and cultural relevance influencers wield and realized the price of reaching their audience is surprisingly cheap. You get what you pay for.

Tech.title: Lenovo’s Legion Go S with SteamOS is down to its lowest price ever
Tech.content:
Memory and storage prices will be inflated for the foreseeable future, so we’re always happy to find a good deal on capable gaming hardware, like this discount on the Lenovo Legion Go S with a Z2 Go processor and SteamOS. Normally $1,137.41 (and selling for close to $1,000 at Best Buy ), Lenovo has the handheld console on sale for just $635.54 when you use code EXTRASAVEAFF at checkout, the lowest price we’ve seen yet for this model.

We reviewed both the Windows and SteamOS versions of this gaming handheld when it released in 2024, and found the latter to be a much more appealing option, largely thanks to the improved user experience that Windows has shown signs that it’s slowly catching up to.
